title: Basis for preparation of the report
heading: 1.1. Basis for preparation of the report
start_phrase: OTP Bank Plc. has also prepared its CSRD Sustainability Statement (in accordance with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, ESRS) at the individual level, covering the individual operations of the parent bank (hereinafter “the Bank”, “OTP Bank”), with the same scope as the individual -level financial statement.
summary:
- Scope and purpose: Stand-alone CSRD/ESRS Sustainability Statement for OTP Bank Plc. at the individual (parent bank) level, aligned with the scope of its individual financial statements; the Group’s consolidated sustainability report is published separately.
- Reporting basis and compliance: Prepared under ESRS (ESRS 2 BP-1 and BP-2). Complies with Hungarian Accounting Law requirements for XHTML/ESEF format; XBRL tagging not applied because an ESEF sustainability taxonomy has not yet been adopted. No omissions for intellectual property or negotiations. First-time ESRS individual reporting, so no prior-period comparatives; definition of material error provided. Forward-looking uncertainty acknowledged but not separately disclosed. No other standards’ indicators presented. Disclosures by reference are listed in the ESRS Index; phasing-in option applied with items identified in the Index.
- Value chain and materiality: Group-level double materiality, covering upstream and downstream value chain, is applied to the Bank at individual level. Time horizons, estimation approaches, and uncertainty handling align with Group methodology.
- Governance structure (ESRS 2 GOV-1): Governance bodies mirror the Group’s—Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, Audit Committee, and other permanent/special committees. Composition, experience, and diversity details are referenced to the Group Sustainability Report and the individual financial report.
- Sustainability governance: An ESG organisation established in 2021 covers the entire Group, including the Bank. ESG Committee and ESG Sub-Committee are permanent; roles, responsibilities, reporting lines, and measures to ensure sustainability expertise are defined.
- Business conduct (ESRS G1 GOV-1): Ethical conduct overseen by the Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, and Ethics Committee. Strong focus on anti–money laundering with a dedicated Money Laundering Prevention Committee. Compliance oversight rests with the Board and Supervisory Board.
- Governance information flows and remuneration (ESRS 2 GOV-2): Sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities are communicated through integrated channels consistent with Group practices. Risk management, strategic decision processes, and executive remuneration follow Group policies.
- Incentives (ESRS 2 GOV-3, E1 GOV-3): Remuneration Policy includes an ESG-CSR indicator encompassing climate considerations; no explicit GHG emissions reduction target is used in incentive benchmarking.
text:
1. Basis for preparation of the report  
ESRS3 2 BP -1: General basis for preparing sustainability statements  
OTP Bank Plc. has also prepared its CSRD Sustainability Statement (in accordance with the European 
Sustainability Reporting Standards, ESRS) at the individual level, covering the individual operations of the 
parent bank (hereinafter “the Bank”, “OTP Bank”), with the same scope as the individual -level financial 
statement.  
The consolidated Management Report covering the entire Banking Group (hereinafter referred to as 'the 
Group', 'OTP Group') is available in the OTP Group's sustainability report (OTP Group Sustainability report)  
Company names used in the report:  
• OTP Bank Plc.: OTP Bank, the Bank  
• a consolidated group of companies: OTP Group, Banking Group, Group  
OTP Bank has not made use of the possibility to omit specific information corresponding to intellectual 
property, know -how or innovation results, nor has it made use of the exemption from disclosure of information 
on pending developments or matters under n egotiation.  
Section 95/I (1) of the Hungarian Accounting Law requires that the Company must prepare its business report 
including the sustainability statement in the electronic reporting format (XHTML) set out in Commission 
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/815(ESEF Regulation), and the sustainability disclosures defined by the 
ESEF taxonomy, including those required according to article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852, must be tagged 
in the sustainability statement using the XBRL markup language. Given that the ESEF taxono my for 
sustainability reporting has not been adopted yet, the Company, was unable to carry out the XBRL tagging.  
Managing the value chain  
OTP Bank's materiality analysis at group level took into account the material impacts, risks and opportunities 
relating to its upstream and downstream value chain. As the parent company of the banking group, OTP Bank 
Plc. played a key role in the materiali ty assessment, so the relevance of the value chain assessed for the 
Group should be interpreted at an individual level as well (for more details on the coverage of the value chain, 
please refer to subsection 1.1. Basis for preparation of the report in the OTP Group Sustainability Report).  
ESRS 2 BP -2: Disclosures relating to specific circumstances  
The time horizons, value chain estimation and actionment uncertainty information defined by OTP Bank at the 
individual level are consistent with the methodology used by the Group (see subsection 1.1. Basis for 
preparation of the report in the OTP Group Sustainability Report).  
This is the first time that OTP Bank discloses sustainability information at an individual level as well, as required 
by ESRS, so no change from the previous period can be identified and therefore no revised comparative figure 
is available (see subsection 1.1. Basis for preparation of the report in the OTP Group Sustainability Report).  
Forward -looking information always carries a certain degree of uncertainty, which is not separately 
disclosed.  
For the previous period, a material error is considered to be one which, on the basis of an individual 
assessment of the error and under reasonable assumption, could affect the user's decisions made on the basis 
of the Sustainability Statement.  
No other reporting standard indicators are presented in the sustainability report prepared at the individual level.  
Disclosures that are incorporated by reference are displayed in the ESRS content index table (see section 5. 
ESRS Index).  
The Bank has made use of the phasing -in option in its individual -level sustainability report, and the ESRS 
content index table (see section 5. ESRS Index) shows the sustainability subtopics and items for which it has 
applied this in the first reporting per iod. F or more detail see subsection ESRS 2 BP -2 Disclosures relating to 
specific circumstances in the OTP Group sustainability report.  
 
3 European Sustainability Reporting Standards

INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  27 1.

title: Governance
heading: 1.2. Governance
start_phrase: The management, executive and supervisory bodies of OTP Bank Plc. are the Supervisory Board, the Board of Directors and all their committees, including the Audit Committee and the special and permanent committees listed in the Responsible Corporate Governance Report, which are the same as the management bodies of the OTP Group.
summary:
- Governance structure and oversight: OTP Bank Plc.’s governing bodies comprise the Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, Audit Committee, and permanent/special committees, aligned with OTP Group structures. Composition, diversity, and experience of these bodies are referenced to the OTP Group Sustainability Report.
- Sustainability governance: An ESG organisation established in 2021 operates group-wide, with permanent ESG Committee and ESG Sub-Committee embedded in the Organisational and Operational Rules. Roles, responsibilities, reporting, and measures to ensure sustainability expertise follow group practices.
- Ethical business conduct: The Supervisory Board, Board of Directors, and Ethics Committee oversee ethical conduct and compliance. Anti–money laundering is a key priority, supported by the Money Laundering Prevention Committee. Governance responsibility for compliance rests with the Board and Supervisory Board.
- Information flow to governing bodies: Sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities from materiality assessment are communicated through integrated sectoral channels rather than standalone reports; remuneration policy and executive pay criteria follow OTP Group practices.
- Incentives: The group-level Remuneration Policy includes an ESG-CSR indicator that incorporates sustainability and climate considerations for covered persons; no GHG emission reduction targets are used for benchmarking.
- Due diligence: Elements of due diligence are integrated into group operations, grounded in the Bank’s Compliance Policy.
- Sustainability reporting risk management: The Marketing and Communications Directorate coordinates sustainability reporting, maintains internal controls, collaborates with group functions, and conducts an annual review to identify risks, difficulties, and improvement actions, mirroring consolidated report controls.
- Strategy and business model: OTP Bank is Hungary’s leading credit institution, serving retail, private banking, micro/small, medium/large enterprises, and municipalities via a nationwide branch network and evolving digital/remote channels. It offers deposits and a broad suite of savings and investment products (treasury, government securities, funds, equities, corporate bonds, structured products), aiming for stable liquidity across cycles. The Bank served over 4.3 million customers and employed 10,820 people at end-2024.
- Strategic priorities: Continuous digitalisation, strong emphasis on sustainability to avoid negative and enhance positive impacts, customer-centric products that support financial well-being, commitment to employee well-being, and active roles in financial literacy and cultural development.
- Value chain (upstream): Predominantly services procurement required for operations, especially marketing communications and IT.
text:
2. Governance  
ESRS 2 GOV -1: Role of governing bodies  
Composition and diversity  
The management, executive and supervisory bodies of OTP Bank Plc. are the Supervisory Board, the Board 
of Directors and all their committees, including the Audit Committee and the special and permanent committees 
listed in the Responsible Corporate Governance Report, which are the same as the management bodies of 
the OTP Group. Detailed information on the composition and experience of the governing and supervisory 
bodies can be found in subsection 1.2. Governance – Role of Governing Bodies in the OTP Group 
Sustainability Report, as well as in the individual financial report.  
The composition and the diversity of the Bank's management, executive and supervisory bodies are presented 
in the subsection and table 1.2. Governance – Composition and diversity in the OTP Group Sustainability 
Report.  
Sustainability roles  
In 2021, the Board of Directors decided to establish the bank ESG organisation, whose tasks, responsibilities 
and reporting obligations cover the whole Group, thus also covering the operations of OTP Bank. The ESG 
Committee and the ESG Sub -Committee have b een included as permanent committees in the Organisational 
and Operational Rules, the tasks of the relevant organisational units and specialised areas, their 
responsibilities, reporting obligations and actions taken to ensure sustainability expertise have been defined, 
which are described in detail in subsection 1.2. Governance - Role of Governing Bodies in the OTP Group 
Sustainability Report.  
ESRS G1 GOV -1: Role of governing bodies in business conduct  
The Supervisory Board, the Board of Directors and the Ethics Committee have a prominent role in the 
enforcement of ethical business conduct and compliance. For the Bank, an essential element of responsible 
business conduct is the fight against money launde ring, in which the Money Laundering Prevention Committee 
plays an important role. In terms of compliance, governance and organisational responsibility is taken by the 
Board of Directors and the Supervisory Board.  
For more information on the role of governing bodies in business conduct, please refer to subsection 1.2. 
Governance – The role of governing bodies in business conduct in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
ESRS 2 GOV -2: Informing governing bodies on sustainability  
Information on the impacts, risks and opportunities identified in the materiality assessment is communicated 
in different ways for each topic, not through a separate channel but integrated into sectoral information 
practices. The governing bodies' communication on sustainability, risk management practices and procedures 
for strategic decisions are consistent with those of the OTP Group. The remuneration policy and the criteria 
and details of executive remuneration also follow the Group's practices. More information on these can be 
found in the OTP Group Sustainability Report, subsection 1.2. Governance – Informing governing bodies on 
sustainability.  
ESRS 2 GOV -3, E1 GOV -3: Sustainability and Climate Change in Incentive Mechanisms  
A summary of the remuneration system specific to OTP Bank can be found in subsection 1.2. Governance – 
Sustainability in incentive mechanisms in the OTP Group Sustainability Report, which describes the main 
guidelines of the Remuneration Policy  developed by the parent bank and followed at group level. The Policy 
includes considerations related to sustainability and climate change targets, which are taken into account as 
part of the “Environmental and Social Responsibility (ESG -CSR)” indicator.  
Climate considerations are taken into account as part of this indicator for persons covered by the Policy. No 
GHG emission reduction target is included in the benchmarking.   
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (STAND -ALONE ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  28 ESRS 2 GOV -4: Due diligence  
In OTP Bank's operations, certain elements of the due diligence process are integrated into the Group's 
operations (not as a separate and interrelated process).  
The Bank acts in accordance with its Compliance Policy, which also serves as the basis for group -wide 
practices, as described in detail in subsection 1.2, Governance – Due diligence in the OTP Group Sustainability 
Report.  
ESRS 2 GOV -5: Risk management in relation to sustainability reporting  
The sustainability reporting process (both at individual and group level) is coordinated by the Marketing and 
Communications Directorate of OTP Bank, which is responsible for the development and operation of internal 
controls. As an important tool for risk  management and internal control procedures, reporting is carried out in 
close engaging with the parent bank's business areas and, based on the OTP Group's governance model, 
OTP Bank, as the parent company, provides strategic control and professional/funct ional guidance and 
cooperates with the group members.  
Following the annual reporting, OTP Bank's Marketing and Communications Directorate assesses the 
sustainability reporting process and reviews the risks arising from the expected changes in the next period. 
This assessment also covers the technical, adminis trative and substantive conditions for reporting. The factors 
causing difficulties and risks are identified, and steps for improvement are defined. The risks identified and the 
control actions taken to address them are realised similarly to those used in t he preparation of the consolidated 
report (see subsection 1.2. Governance – Risk management in relation to sustainability reporting in the OTP 
Group Sustainability Report).

title: Strategy
heading: 1.3. Strategy
start_phrase: OTP Bank is the leading credit institution in Hungary.
summary:
- Governance and due diligence (ESRS 2 GOV-4, GOV-5)
  - Due diligence elements are embedded in group operations and guided by OTP Group’s Compliance Policy.
  - Sustainability reporting is coordinated by OTP Bank’s Marketing and Communications Directorate, which oversees internal controls, collaborates closely with business areas and group members, and provides strategic/functional guidance.
  - After each annual cycle, the Directorate reviews reporting processes, identifies risks and obstacles (technical/administrative/substantive), and defines improvement steps, aligned with the consolidated reporting approach.

- Strategy, business model and value chain (ESRS 2 SBM-1)
  - OTP Bank is Hungary’s leading credit institution, serving retail, private banking, MSME, corporate (mid/large), and municipal clients via branches and evolving digital/remote channels.
  - Offers deposits and a broad suite of savings/investment and treasury products (incl. government securities, funds, equities, corporate bonds, structured investments).
  - Strategic focus on stable liquidity across cycles, continuous digitalisation, accessibility, security, and sustainability (avoiding negative impacts, realising positives, and customer well-being).
  - Workforce and reach: 10,820 employees and over 4.3 million customers in Hungary at end-2024.

- Value chain highlights
  - Upstream: service procurement dominates (marketing communications, IT, telecom); operational real estate includes intra-group and leased properties; company cars typically owned within the group.
  - Downstream: strong agency (third-party) sales, especially mortgage brokerage; 58% of OTP Bank product sales in 2024 via third parties; 477 dependent agents at OTP Financial Point are counted in own workforce per ESRS.
  - Most significant environmental and social impacts arise through customers, mainly via lending.
  - As parent, OTP Bank steers and coordinates group practices (including ESG); group policies extend group-wide while allowing local initiatives.

- ESG strategy
  - OTP Bank leads the group’s four-year ESG strategy (adopted 2021) to be a regional leader in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low-carbon economy and enabling ethical, socially and environmentally sound financial choices.

- Stakeholders (ESRS 2 SBM-2)
  - Corporate and ESG strategies prioritise customers, investors, employees, and broader stakeholders.
  - Code of Ethics mandates ethical conduct for all employees and agents.
  - Ongoing engagement with subsidiaries, clients, investors/analysts, employees, regulators, NGOs/professional bodies, sponsored organisations, education/research institutions, the public, suppliers, and competitors through surveys, meetings, reporting, and consultations.
  - Feedback informs strategy, services, products, and programs; governing bodies receive regular stakeholder-related reports.
  - Note: materiality assessment and due diligence did not specifically examine stakeholder views on the strategy and business model.

- Materiality assessment (ESRS 2; topical E1–E5, G1 IRO-1)
  - OTP Bank’s analysis builds on the Group’s ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment; for individual reporting, it focuses on impacts, risks, and opportunities from financial services.
  - Group identified three activity scopes: financial services (most prominent), real estate, and agriculture; the latter two are not relevant for OTP Bank.
  - Assessment emphasised areas with heightened risk of adverse impacts; no new OTP Bank–specific impacts beyond group-level findings.
  - Stakeholder inputs included ESG ratings/questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s), TRI*M customer surveys, a 2024 employee engagement survey (8,596 responses; 79% response rate), and an online stakeholder questionnaire (NGOs, academia, authorities/regulators, analysts/stock exchanges, media, employee representatives).
  - Based on feedback, “employees: work-life balance” was added as a material topic; financial analysts and market stakeholders informed financial materiality.

3. Strategy  
ESRS 2 SBM -1: Strategy, business model and value chain  
Business model, products and services  
OTP Bank is the leading credit institution in Hungary. OTP Bank's business model is focused on providing a 
high level of service to the financial needs of Hungarian retail, private banking, micro and small enterprises, 
medium and large enterprises and municipal customers through the Bank's branch network and the constantly 
evolving digital and innovative remote service channels, with a focus on ease of use a nd reliability. The Bank 
offers a wide range of modern banking and financial services to both retail and corporate customers, collecting 
demand and fixed deposits from customers and offering a wide range of other savings products, including, 
country depend ent treasury services, treasury services, government securities, investment funds, equities and 
corporate bonds, as well as other securities and structured investments. In line with the strategy, the Bank 
aims to maintain a stable liquidity position across  economic cycles to ensure conditions for stable operations 
and growth. The Bank and the other domestic members of the Group served the financial needs of more than 
4.3 million customers at the end of 2024. A detailed description of the financial services provided by the 
Banking Group and the related data are presented in the OTP Group Sustainability Report, section 1.3. 
Strategy, subsection ESRS 2 SBM -1: Strategy, business model and value chain.  
The Bank aims to continuously improve its services in a constantly evolving digital and technological 
environment, so that they are clear and easily accessible and secure for a broader range of customers. In 
addition to digitalisation, OTP Bank places a st rong emphasis on sustainability, aiming to avoid negative 
environmental and social impacts, realise positive impacts and leverage potential business benefits. The Bank 
is committed to offering products that are tailored to the real needs of its customers, in line with their capabilities 
and contribute to their financial well -being.  
Our employees are a key asset, and their high performance is a guarantee of OTP Bank's results. As a 
responsible employer, the aim is to improve employee well -being. The Bank plays an active role in developing 
the financial awareness of the population and enriching cultural values.  
OTP Bank in Hungary employed 10,820 people at the end of 2024.   
Value chain  
Upstream value chain  
The core business of OTP Bank is the provision of financial services, and, in the value chain part preceding 
this activity, suppliers of products and services necessary for its operations, products and services are 
appearing. Procurement of services dominates, in particular marketing communications, IT and  MANAGEMENT REPORT (STAND -ALONE ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  29 telecommunications services. The real -estate used for operational purposes includes both intra -group property 
and leased space. Company cars are typically owned within the group.  
 
Downstream value chain  
This includes the value chain part following OTP Bank's activities, those involved in the sale of products and 
services, and those who use the products and services, i.e. customers.  The agency channel (third -party sales 
channel) plays an essential role in the intermediation of financial services. Within the agency sales channel, 
mortgage brokerage is the most important product. In 2024, OTP Bank's third -party sales within product 
reached 58% of the contracted amount.  The agents of OTP Financial Point (477 persons), who are dependent 
agents working as self -employed persons and broker the products of OTP Bank, are included in own workforce 
under the ESRS (see Materiality assessment  ESRS2 SBM -3). 
 
The Bank's most significant environmental and social impacts are experienced through its financial services 
customers, mainly in the area of lending which is the most impactful part of the value chain.  
 
OTP Bank is part of the OTP Banking Group, which has domestic and foreign subsidiaries, most of which are 
active in the provision of financial services, but there are also entities active in other sectors such as property 
management and agriculture. The do uble materiality assessment conducted at group level has fully considered 
the  activities of the subsidiaries. For OTP Bank, the impacts and risks identified pertain to its financial services 
activities.  OTP Bank, as the parent bank of the Banking Group, plays a steering and coordinating role in most 
areas (typically also in ESG issues), while at the same time it provides opportunities for subsidiary banks to 
channel and implement their own initiatives. T he policies related to the material topics are extended at group 
level, and, for the related actions, the specificities of the subsidiary banks and the group -level indicators are 
presented in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
ESG strategy  
OTP Bank plays a leading role in the development and implementation of the group -level sustainability 
strategy (four -year ESG strategy adopted in 2021), the main target of which is to ensure that the Group is a 
regional leader in financing a fair and gradu al transition to a low -carbon economy and to support ethical, 
socially and environmentally sound financial choices through responsible solutions.  
The Banking Group's ESG strategy (vision, mission, goals and challenges) is detailed in subsection 1.3. 
Strategy – Strategy, business model and value chain – ESG strategy in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
ESRS 2 SBM -2: Stakeholders  
OTP Bank's group -wide corporate strategy (see the Corporate Strategy section of the consolidated 
Management Report ) aims to serve the needs and expectations of its customers, investors and employees at 
the highest possible level.  
In addition, the Group's ESG strategy expresses the commitment of the Group and its members to act as 
responsible partners with all its stakeholders, as reflected in the three pillars of the strategy: responsible service 
provider, responsible employer and responsible social actor.  
The Code of Ethics of the OTP Group states that the aim is to apply the principles of ethical business conduct 
in relations with stakeholders, and that compliance with these principles is a mandatory requirement for all 
employees and agents4. 
The Bank cooperates with its key stakeholders, and seeking their views is a priority, as meeting their 
expectations ensures the Bank's social legitimacy and business success. It continuously seeks and takes into 
account feedback in the design and developme nt of its strategy, activities and programmes.  
The materiality assessment and due diligence did not explore the views and interests of stakeholders on the 
strategy and business model.

title: Materiality assessment
heading: 1.4. Materiality assessment
start_phrase: The purpose of the materiality assessment is to enable OTP Bank to identify material impacts, risks and opportunities arising from its activities.
summary:
- Purpose and scope: Describes OTP Bank’s materiality assessment to identify material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, using a double materiality approach aligned with ESRS and based on the OTP Group’s group-level methodology.
- Group-to-entity alignment: OTP Bank, as parent, leverages the Group’s top-down double materiality analysis; no new bank-specific impacts were identified beyond group-level. Of the Group’s three activity scopes (financial services, real estate, agriculture), only financial services are material for the Bank’s standalone reporting.
- Methodology references: Points to the OTP Group Sustainability Report for detailed methods on identifying and assessing impacts, risks, and opportunities, including climate-related topics.
- Stakeholder engagement: Incorporates inputs from ESG rating questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s), national retail TRI*M brand/satisfaction surveys, an employee engagement survey (8,596 responses; 79% response rate), and an online stakeholder questionnaire (NGOs, academia, authorities/regulators, analysts, media, employee reps). Work–life balance was added as a material topic based on feedback.
- Financial risks and opportunities identification: Began with ESRS themes, SASB for financials, and ESG assessment topics; workshops and expert consultations prioritized a short list and considered short/medium/long-term horizons; no additional bank-specific risks/opportunities beyond group-level.
- Validation and governance: Internal reviews included near-threshold topics corrected with stakeholder feedback; Hungarian and foreign subsidiaries commented. The ESG Sub-Committee approved the final list (with one modification).
- Key material topics (ESRS 2 SBM-3) and responses:
  - Climate (E1): Mitigation and adaptation are material. Scope 3 portfolio emissions dominate; Scope 1–2 are smaller but significant overall. A loan portfolio decarbonization (transition) plan was prepared by end-2024; Scope 1–2 reduction plans are being developed, with green electricity a key lever. Green lending presents major opportunities; transition and physical risks are managed within ESG risk frameworks and stress testing.
  - Energy: Financing energy-intensive and fossil-fuel users creates credit/reputational risks; opportunities in renewables and energy efficiency through green lending.
  - Water (E3): Exposure via clients in high water-withdrawal sectors; minimum compliance expectations set, with ongoing deeper assessment to inform future expectations; potential financial risks if clients cannot meet evolving requirements.
  - Biodiversity (E4): Potential negative client impacts in certain sectors; current focus on legal compliance and permits, with further understanding to shape expectations; biodiversity not considered financially material for resilience assessment at this stage.
  - Own workforce (S1): Material subtopics include work–life balance, health and safety (noting stress risks), gender equality and equal pay (generally small gaps in same roles; lower female representation at higher levels), training and skills (broad access; room for improvement in consistency), employment of persons with disabilities (low current levels; anti-discrimination in place but limited targeted measures), anti-violence/harassment measures, and wider diversity.
  - Consumers/end-users (S4): Information security, data protection and cyber defense are critical; ongoing system, process, and training enhancements; residual risks remain. Access to quality information and to financial products/services (including digital access and state-supported mortgages) are material, with continuous improvements and remaining gaps.
  - Business conduct (G1): Corporate culture, compliance, and AML/CFT are central, supported by code of ethics, whistleblowing, and mandatory trainings; residual risks of non-compliance exist. Anti-corruption practices include training, clauses for partners, and risk assessments, acknowledging potential for isolated abuse.
- Risk and resilience insights: No provisions or capital buffers were set for ESG-related risks in 2024; ESG-flagging applied in operational loss data collection; no significant ESG-related losses realized in 2024. Climate stress testing conducted; biodiversity/ecosystem resilience not performed due to limited financial materiality. Further financial impact analysis planned for 2025.
- Reporting approach and ESRS coverage: OTP Bank’s standalone disclosures follow group-developed data collection and reporting practices, mapped to ESRS and EFRAG guidance (ID 177/AR16). Entity-specific disclosures are prioritized for information security/data protection, quality information, access to financial products/services, and business conduct/AML; value-chain topics (water withdrawal; direct drivers of biodiversity loss) are material with entity-specific disclosures to be developed. Use of phase-in options and a consolidated ESRS Index are referenced.

4. Materiality assessment  
ESRS 2, E1, E2, E3, E4, E5, G1 IRO -1 
The purpose of the materiality assessment is to enable OTP Bank to identify material impacts, risks and 
opportunities arising from its activities. The materiality assessment focused on the question of whether a topic 
is material, with the depth of the assessment of each impact, risk and opportunity bein g done with this in mind.  
The materiality analysis of OTP Bank is based on the double materiality analysis prepared at the level of the 
Banking Group. The methodology for the process of identifying and assessing impacts, risks and opportunities 
for the group -level reporting process  has been developed in line with the ESRS requirements.  
OTP Bank, as the parent bank, played a key role in identifying material impacts, risks and opportunities in the 
Group's dual materiality analysis. Building on the Group's top -down approach to materiality analysis at the 
consolidated level, OTP Bank, in rel ation to its own operations, considers the impacts, risks and opportunities 
identified in the provision of financial services as its core business as the basis for its reporting at the individual 
level.  
The methodology of the dual materiality analysis of the Banking Group is described in detail in chapter 1.4 
Materiality Assessment of the OTP Group Sustainability Report and  related to the assessment of climate 
change -related topics can also be found in section 1.4 Materiality Assessment of the OTP Group Sustainability 
Report  
Identifying and assessing impacts  
E1 IRO -1, E2 IRO -1, E3 IRO -1, E4 IRO -1, E5 IRO -1, G1 -IRO-1  
The materiality assessment focused on factors that are associated with an increased risk of adverse impacts. 
The scope of activities was a good starting point for identifying the increased risk of adverse impacts, thus, 
OTP Group grouped its subsidiaries by scope of activities, along which it identified the im pacts related to its 
own activities and value chain. Regarding OTP Bank no new impacts have been identified; all group -level 
impacts are applicable to the Bank as well.  
The OTP Group has identified three relevant scopes of activity: the most prominent are (1) financial services; 
followed by (2) real -estate and (3) agriculture.  
OTP's group -level assessment includes the member companies related to the Bank's operations (as internal 
members of its value chain, thus providing a more complete picture of the Bank's operational scope). Thus, 
the Bank relies on the group -level assessmen t in its individual reporting, however, the impacts identified in the 
agricultural and real -estate sectors are not relevant for the Bank.  
The methodology of the process for identifying and assessing impacts, risks and opportunities is described in 
detail in section 1.4 Materiality assessment of the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
Consultation with stakeholders  
E2 IRO -1, E3 IRO -1, E4 IRO -1, E5 IRO -1 
The Bank has used a wide range of sources to understand the views and expectations of stakeholders and 
has taken them into account in identifying and assessing material impacts at group level.  
Among other things, we have used:  
− ESG assessments, questionnaires: Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s.  
− Retail TRI*M Index surveys (nationally representative residential survey) measuring brand, 
satisfaction and loyalty.  
− Employee engagement surveys, with a particular focus on OTP Bank’s engagement survey relating 
to 2024, with 8,596 responses and a 79% response rate.  
 
For its materiality assessment, it also took into account the views of NGOs, universities; public authorities, 
regulators, public administrations; financial analysts, stock exchanges; media; employee representatives, as 
requested through an online stakehol der questionnaire. Based on the feedback, one topic was included in the 
list of material topics (employees: work -life balance), as it was considered material by more than a third of the 
respondents. The views of financial analysts and stock market stakehol ders were also sought from a financial 
materiality perspective.    MANAGEMENT REPORT (STAND -ALONE ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  32 Identifying and assessing financial risks and opportunities  
The identification of financial risks and opportunities for sustainability issues was the result of an iterative 
process.  
As a starting point for identifying financial risks and opportunities (long list):  
- we used the themes identified by the ESRS  
- adding the source points also used for the impact materiality,  
- the SASB standards for the financial sector, and  
- ESG assessment topics.  
Based on the last two sources, there was no need to add a new topic.  
Sustainability issues where a relevant risk or opportunity (either from impacts or dependencies) may arise for 
the OTP Group (short list) were identified through a workshop and subsequent consultations with the 
assistance of OTP Bank's experts. Participant s considered whether the risks and opportunities are relevant in 
the short, medium or long term , furthermore no additional risks or opportunities have been identified from OTP 
Bank’s perspective.  
 
For the methodology of a more in -depth exploration and assessment of the risks and opportunities arising from 
the relevant topics, please refer to subsection 1.4. Materiality assessment – Identification and assessment of 
financial risks and opportunities in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
Validation of the assessment and approval  
The assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities was followed by a series of internal reviews. This included 
a review of the assessment of impacts below the materiality threshold, but close to it, in relation to the results 
corrected with stakeholder fee dback. The Hungarian subsidiaries as well as the relevant representatives of 
foreign subsidiaries provided feedback on the materiality assessment.  
The ESG Sub -Committee discussed the list of material impacts, risks and opportunities and approved it by 
majority decision, subject to one modification, in accordance with the Sub -Committee's rules of procedure.

INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  40 The material sustainability impacts identified by the OTP Group, which are related to financial services 
(mostly lending activities), have been identified as impacts, risks and opportunities that are also 
assessed as relevant to the core business of OTP Bank. The material impacts identified by the OTP 
Group are detailed in subsection 1.4. Materiality assessment – Material sustainability impacts of the 
OTP Group in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
As regards the management of the potential financial impact of ESG -related risks, no provision was 
made for ESG -related risks during 2024 and no capital buffer was set by the management for such risks. 
Operational risks are flagged (ESG flag) in the contex t of loss data collection if an ESG risk factor can 
be identified behind the loss event. No significant losses on material issues were realised in 2024. An 
analysis of the expected financial impacts and an estimate of the expected financial impacts will be  
made in 2025.  
OTP Bank's risk management processes, prudent behaviour and business planning practices ensure 
its resilience to manage sustainability impacts, risks and take opportunities. The Bank, as part of the 
Group, carried out a stress test to assess the potential impact of climate change, which was justified by 
both regulatory and business considerations (see subsection 2.4.2. Credit Risk – Stress test in the OTP 
Group Sustainability Report). No resilience assessment was carried out for the biodiversity and 
ecosyst em themes, which were not considered to be financially material. Addressing complex 
environmental challenges adequately also requires the involvement of the banking sector, and further 
resilience analyses are likely to be warranted in the future. The Bank continuously monitors market 
opportunities to take advantage of them and keeps abreast of regulatory requirements to ensure that it 
can respond appropriately.  
OTP Bank has not previously prepared a sustainability report at an individual level, its activities were 
presented as part of the group -level consolidated report, in accordance with GRI Standard 2021.  
OTP Bank follows the application of group -level entity specific disclosures (@ ESRS Index ) to 
characterise the impact of the following material topics:  
• Water withdrawal – material regarding the value chain, entity -specific disclosure will be 
developed later  
• Direct drivers of biodiversity loss – material regarding the value chain, entity -specific 
disclosure will be developed later  
• Information security and data protection  
• Quality information  
• Access to financial products and services  
• Corporate culture, compliance, fight against money laundering

title: List of ESRS requirements covered and general reporting policy
heading: 1.5. List of ESRS requirements covered and general reporting policy
start_phrase: In preparing its sustainability statement, OTP Bank has determined the list of disclosure requirements based on the results of the materiality assessment carried out by the Group, which are also relevant at an individual level.
summary:
- Scope and materiality: OTP Bank’s stand‑alone report aligns with OTP Group’s materiality assessment, focusing on sustainability impacts tied to financial services (primarily lending). Detailed impact mapping is referenced to the Group Sustainability Report (section 1.4).

- ESG risk management: No provisions or capital buffers for ESG-related risks were set in 2024. Operational loss events are ESG-flagged where relevant; no significant ESG-related losses occurred in 2024. The Bank plans to analyze and estimate expected financial impacts in 2025.

- Resilience and stress testing: Existing risk management and planning processes support resilience to sustainability risks and opportunities. A climate change stress test was conducted for regulatory and business reasons. No biodiversity/ecosystem resilience assessment was performed, as these were not considered financially material, though further analyses may be warranted.

- Market and regulatory readiness: The Bank monitors evolving market opportunities and regulatory requirements to respond appropriately.

- Reporting evolution: Previously, OTP Bank reported only at Group level under GRI 2021; this is a stand‑alone report drawing on Group methodologies.

- Entity-specific topics followed from Group ESRS approach: 
  - Water withdrawal (material in value chain; disclosure to be developed)
  - Direct drivers of biodiversity loss (material in value chain; disclosure to be developed)
  - Information security and data protection
  - Quality information
  - Access to financial products and services
  - Corporate culture, compliance, and anti–money laundering

- ESRS reporting policy (ESRS 2 IRO‑2): Disclosures are selected based on Group materiality but applied at Bank level. The parent bank coordinates Group-wide data collection and methodologies, follows EFRAG guidance (ID 177) for linking data points, and uses a structured approach (Data Points, Policy, Action, Target, Metrics, Entity‑specific Disclosures). Where applicable, information is cross‑referenced to the Group report. Phase‑in options and a detailed ESRS Index are provided in chapter 5.

statement and general reporting policy in the OTP Group Sustainability Report), covering OTP Bank

presented b y referring back to the group -level report.

summary:
- Context and scope: This section of the standalone Management Report (Integrated Annual Report 2024) provides environmental information focused on EU Taxonomy disclosures for a credit institution under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation. It reports as of 31 December 2024.

- KPI summary under the EU Taxonomy:
  - Main KPI – Green Asset Ratio (GAR, stock):
    - Environmentally sustainable assets: HUF 21,669 million (turnover-based) and HUF 66,252 million (capex-based).
    - Reported GAR values: 0.17% (turnover-based) and 0.51% (capex-based).
    - High exclusions: a significant share of assets excluded from GAR numerator and denominator per Article 7 and Annex V.
  - Additional KPIs – GAR (flow):
    - Environmentally sustainable activities: HUF 8,779 million (turnover-based) and HUF 33,225 million (capex-based).
    - Reported values: 0.32% (turnover-based) and 1.20% (capex-based).
    - Exclusions remain high in the numerator (around 90%) and material in the denominator (around 10–23%).
  - Financial guarantees and Assets under Management: reported as zero.
  - Note on scope: Fees/Commissions and Trading Book KPIs will apply starting 2026; SME inclusion subject to a positive impact assessment.

- GAR asset base and coverage – turnover-based:
  - Total assets: HUF 18,925,227 million.
  - Total GAR assets: HUF 12,915,794 million.
  - Assets covered in both numerator and denominator (loans, debt securities, equity not HfT): HUF 6,588,317 million, with taxonomy-eligible and aligned amounts disclosed by environmental objective.
  - Assets excluded from numerator (but in denominator): HUF 6,327,477 million, including:
    - SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD: HUF 2,846,798 million.
    - Non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD: HUF 200,740 million.
    - Derivatives, on-demand interbank, cash and other assets.
  - Assets not covered for GAR calculation: HUF 6,009,433 million (central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, trading book).
  - Counterparty breakdown includes financial undertakings (notably credit institutions), non-financial undertakings, and households (with details for residential mortgages and building renovation loans).

- GAR asset base and coverage – capex-based:
  - Same total assets and GAR asset base as turnover view.
  - Higher taxonomy-aligned amounts relative to turnover-based view, especially within non-financial undertakings.
  - Detailed split of environmentally sustainable exposures by environmental objective (Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation dominate; Water, Circular Economy, Pollution, Biodiversity minimal or zero).
  - Households reported similarly (including renovation loans), with no additional taxonomy alignment under capex.

- Environmental objectives detail:
  - Disclosures distinguish taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned exposures across six objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity (BIO).
  - Reported aligned amounts are concentrated in Climate Change Mitigation; minor amounts in Adaptation; negligible in Water, CE, PPC, BIO.

- Household and collateral specifics:
  - Households include loans collateralised by residential property and building renovation loans (with renovation loans explicitly identified).
  - No motor vehicle loans reported as taxonomy-relevant.

- Sectoral (NACE-4) breakdown – turnover-based:
  - Provides a granular mapping of non-financial corporates (subject to NFRD) vs SMEs/other NFCs into CCM/CCA/WTR eligibility and alignment.
  - Sectors represented include energy and utilities (e.g., 3511–3514), transport and logistics (e.g., 4931, 4950), financial and holding activities (6420, 6492, 7010), selected manufacturing codes, real estate (6820), and others, with aligned amounts indicated where applicable.

- Reporting notes and methodology:
  - Uses both counterparty Turnover KPI and CapEx KPI consistent with Delegated Acts; for general lending, turnover KPI is applied.
  - Clarifies treatment of use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities (mostly limited amounts).
  - All figures presented in HUF million with coverage percentages over total assets and specified exclusions aligned to Article 7 and Annex V of the Taxonomy disclosures.

summary:
- Extract from the Management Report (Stand‑Alone) of the Integrated Annual Report 2024 presenting Section 2: GAR (Green Asset Ratio) sector information.
- Provides mandatory EU Taxonomy disclosures split by:
  - Basis: Turnover-based GAR and Capex-based GAR.
  - Environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Counterparty types: Non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs SMEs and other non‑financial corporates not subject to NFRD.
  - Sector granularity: NACE Rev. 2, 4‑digit code and label.
- For each NACE sector, shows gross carrying amounts (HUF million) and the portion that is environmentally sustainable for each objective, plus a total across all objectives.
- Turnover-based table highlights sectors with notable environmentally sustainable exposure, including electricity activities (3511–3514), activities of head offices (7010), holding companies (6420), manufacture of starches and starch products (1062), gas distribution/trade (3522–3523), and urban/suburban land transport (4931), while several sectors show minimal or zero alignment.
- Capex-based table indicates high taxonomy-aligned capex in head offices (7010), holding companies (6420), electricity generation/transmission/distribution (3511–3513), chemicals (2059), urban transport (4931), and others; many sectors have limited or no aligned capex.
- All amounts are disclosed in HUF million and distinguish between taxonomy-eligible exposures and the subset that is environmentally sustainable (aligned), serving as inputs to the institution’s GAR.

summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for 2024 within the Management Report, focusing on:
  - Section 2: Capex-based GAR sector information by NACE 4-digit codes.
    - For each sector, gross carrying amounts (HUF million) are shown for exposures to non-financial corporates subject to NFRD and to SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
    - Breakdowns cover the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), with “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts for each.
    - Data indicate CCM dominates the environmentally sustainable capex; CCA, WTR, PPC, and BIO show minimal values, with CE contributing modest amounts in select sectors.
    - Notable CCM concentrations (by code) include 7010, 6420, 3511, 2059, 1062, 4931, and 3512; several sectors record zeros or very small sustainable amounts.
    - A total column aggregates environmentally sustainable capex across all six objectives for each sector.
  - Section 3: GAR KPI Stock – Turnover-based data (as of 31 December 2024).
    - Reports percentages relative to total covered assets, distinguishing taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned exposures for CCM, CCA, and WTR.
    - Breakdowns by counterparty/instrument class: financial undertakings (incl. credit institutions), non-financial undertakings, households, local governments; and by asset type (loans, debt securities, equity).
    - For CCM, taxonomy-aligned exposures are further split into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling; for CCA/WTR, into use-of-proceeds and enabling.
    - Key figures: non-financial undertakings show 10.6% taxonomy-eligible and 6.6% taxonomy-aligned under CCM (with 1.8% transitional and 3.7% enabling); households include taxonomy-relevant categories such as residential mortgages (33.5%) and building renovation loans (100%) though aligned shares are 0.0%.
    - Overall total GAR assets reflect low taxonomy exposure on a turnover basis: 0.5% taxonomy-eligible and 0.2% taxonomy-aligned under CCM, with negligible CCA and WTR.

title: GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based data
heading: 3. GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based data
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
- Extract from the Integrated Annual Report 2024 (Management Report, Stand‑Alone), section “3. GAR KPI Stock,” disclosing EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) metrics as of 31 December 2024.
- Two GAR Stock views are presented:
  - Turnover-based data (pages 54–55).
  - Capex-based data (page 56).
- Scope and methodology:
  - Results shown for “covered assets in both numerator and denominator.”
  - Breakdown by asset class and counterparty: loans and advances, debt securities (incl. use-of-proceeds), equity instruments (not held for trading), financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations incl. investment firms and management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments (housing/other), and repossessed collateral.
  - Disaggregation by EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), Biodiversity (BIO).
  - Distinguishes taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned exposures, and within aligned: use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Coverage:
  - Proportion of total assets covered by GAR denominator: 68.25%.
  - Category coverage examples: loans/debt/equity not HfT 34.81%; credit institutions 18.92%; other financial corporations 4.41%; insurance undertakings 2.43%; households 9.80%.
- Turnover-based key results:
  - Total GAR assets (all objectives combined): ~0.5% taxonomy-eligible; ~0.2% taxonomy-aligned; ~0.1% enabling; negligible use-of-proceeds and transitional overall.
  - Activity concentration in climate objectives; near-zero contributions for WTR, CE, PPC, BIO.
  - Non-financial undertakings show the main contribution (around 10.6–10.9% eligible; 6.6% aligned; split includes ~1.8% transitional and ~3.7% enabling).
  - Households: ~0.9% eligible overall; mortgages flagged as 33.5% eligible within the subcategory; building renovation loans shown as 100% eligible but on a very small base; motor vehicle loans 0%.
  - Financial undertakings, debt securities, and equity instruments: largely 0% eligible/aligned.
- Capex-based key results:
  - Total GAR assets: ~0.9% taxonomy-eligible; ~0.5% taxonomy-aligned; ~0.1% enabling; negligible use-of-proceeds and transitional overall.
  - Higher eligibility/alignment signals for non-financial undertakings vs. turnover view (about 25.0% eligible; 20.5% aligned; ~12.7% transitional; ~3.1% enabling), concentrated in loans and advances.
  - Households figures mirror turnover view (mortgages 33.5% eligible; building renovation loans 100% eligible on minimal exposure).
  - Securities and equity positions remain near 0% across objectives.
- Overall message: GAR coverage is substantial, but taxonomy-eligible and especially aligned exposures remain very low at portfolio level, with contributions concentrated in loans to non-financial corporates and, to a lesser extent, household mortgages/renovation, while securities portfolios, financial counterparties, and non-climate environmental objectives show negligible impact.

summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI Stock disclosures (stand‑alone) as of 31 December 2024, using both capex‑based and turnover‑based data.
- Details percentages of assets that are taxonomy‑eligible and taxonomy‑aligned across environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- Further splits alignments into use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Breaks down exposures by counterparty/asset class: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (including mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments, and collateral obtained.
- Provides the proportion of total assets covered by the GAR denominator (overall coverage shown at 68.2%) and coverage shares for key sub‑portfolios.
- Key findings:
  - Taxonomy‑eligible and aligned exposures are concentrated in loans to non‑financial undertakings, predominantly for climate change mitigation, with smaller shares for adaptation.
  - Households show some eligibility (e.g., residential mortgages and renovation loans) but contribute marginally to the overall GAR.
  - Financial undertakings, local governments, and other categories show minimal to no eligible/aligned exposures.
  - Exposures aligned to WTR, CE, PPC, and BIO are negligible.
  - Turnover‑based GAR results are low overall and generally lower than capex‑based figures, with similar concentration in non‑financial corporates.

title: GAR KPI Stock, – Turnover based data
heading: 4.2. GAR KPI Stock, – Turnover based data
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
- Section 4.2 of the Management Report (Integrated Annual Report 2024) presents the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI Stock as of 31 December 2024, in line with EU Taxonomy disclosures.
- Two GAR views are provided: Turnover-based data and Capex-based data.
- Results are broken down by environmental objectives—Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)—showing:
  - Taxonomy-eligible vs. Taxonomy-aligned proportions
  - “Use of proceeds,” “enabling,” and “transitional” sub-categories (largely zero/negligible)
- Exposures are detailed across counterparty and asset classes included in both numerator and denominator:
  - Loans and advances, debt securities, and equity instruments not held for trading (HfT) eligible for GAR
  - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings)
  - Non-financial undertakings
  - Households (including mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
  - Local governments (housing and other financing)
  - Collateral obtained (residential and commercial property)
- Key outcomes (Turnover-based):
  - Overall GAR totals are very low: around 0.4% taxonomy-eligible and 0.3% taxonomy-aligned across covered assets.
  - Most green exposure is concentrated in non-financial undertakings (notably under CCM); financial sector exposures are largely 0%.
  - Household mortgages show a small taxonomy-eligible share; renovation and vehicle loans are zero.
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR is about 89.5%, with major coverage from loans/debt/equity not HfT eligible.
- Key outcomes (Capex-based):
  - Higher taxonomy shares than turnover-based: total around 1.4% taxonomy-eligible and 1.2% taxonomy-aligned (primarily under CCM).
  - Non-financial undertakings drive the capex-based eligible/aligned exposure; other categories remain near zero.
- The tables provide segment-level proportions of total assets covered, highlighting coverage contributions by each portfolio slice.

title: GAR KPI Stock, – Capex based
heading: 4.2. GAR KPI Stock, – Capex based
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs (CapEx-based) and off-balance sheet KPIs (turnover-based) as of 31 December 2024 within the stand-alone Management Report of the Integrated Annual Report 2024.
- Covers all six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), and splits aligned exposures into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling categories.
- Scope and denominator: GAR metrics apply to covered assets including loans and advances, debt securities, and equity instruments not held for trading (HfT), with detailed breakdowns by counterparty type (financial undertakings, credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments) and by product type (e.g., mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans, collateral obtained).
- Overall results (Total GAR assets):
  - 1.4% of covered assets are taxonomy-eligible and 1.2% are taxonomy-aligned, almost entirely under CCM; within aligned, 1.0% is transitional and 0.1% is enabling; use-of-proceeds is 0.0%.
  - No eligible or aligned exposures reported for CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, or BIO.
  - 89.52% of total assets are covered by the GAR denominator.
- Category highlights:
  - Loans/advances, debt securities, and equity instruments not HfT eligible: 1.9% taxonomy-eligible and 1.6% aligned (1.3% transitional, 0.1% enabling); this category represents 66.05% of total assets covered.
  - Non-financial undertakings: 25.3% taxonomy-eligible and 21.7% aligned (17.3% transitional, 1.4% enabling), concentrated in CCM; category accounts for 4.95% of total assets covered.
  - Households: loans collateralised by residential immovable property show 1.4% taxonomy-eligible under CCM; category represents 13.65% of total assets covered (residential mortgage subset 0.02%).
  - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings) and other listed subcategories report 0.0% taxonomy-eligible/aligned exposures across objectives.
- Off-balance sheet exposures:
  - Financial guarantees KPI and Assets under Management KPI both report 0.00% taxonomy-eligible and 0.00% taxonomy-aligned across all environmental objectives.

title: Climate change and environment
heading: 2.2. Climate change and environment
start_phrase: The impact of OTP Bank arises from direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating climate change.
summary:
- The section centers on Climate Change and Environment, covering mitigation, adaptation, and energy, along with related risks, opportunities, policies, targets, actions, and metrics under ESRS.
- Emissions profile: OTP Bank’s direct (Scope 1–2) emissions are small relative to its financed (Scope 3) emissions, which dominate the footprint. The Bank recognizes both risk exposure (transition and physical) and business opportunities via green finance.
- Green lending strategy and targets:
  - Group ambition to lead financing of a green and just transition; KPI to build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025; green exposure reached HUF 1,027 billion by end-2024.
  - Alignment with EU Taxonomy (mitigation/adaptation). Priority sectors: energy (renewables, grids, storage), real estate (green buildings and deep renovations), and transport (e-mobility). 30.23% of the green portfolio finances renewables.
  - Use of regulatory incentives where possible.
- ESG risk integration: ESG risks embedded in group-level risk policies and processes; corporate lending applies an ESG risk framework since 2021; operational risks addressed via annual Group RCSA and scenario analysis.
- Adaptation: Lending can facilitate clients’ adaptation in sectors like housing, agriculture, real estate, and construction; associated physical and transition risks are managed within the ESG risk framework; Bank aims to capture adaptation-related business opportunities.
- Energy: Financing can reduce clients’ environmental impacts by supporting renewable and green-certified energy; financing fossil- and energy-intensive firms carries credit and reputational risks managed as above.
- Water and biodiversity:
  - Exposure to sectors with high water withdrawal and to activities potentially impacting biodiversity; current minimum expectation is client compliance with environmental and social laws and permits.
  - Deeper analysis underway to refine expectations and potentially set policies; opportunities exist to finance responsible water/biodiversity practices via green lending.
  - No standalone OTP Bank policies or targets yet for water and biodiversity; effectiveness currently not monitored.
- ESRS policy references: Group Credit Risk Policy and Corporate Lending Policy apply; Code of Ethics affirms environmental commitments; detailed policies and methods referenced in the Group Sustainability Report.
- Climate targets and actions:
  - Group plan (2024) to reduce financed GHG emissions by 2030, based on IEA NZE 2050 and national paths; OTP Bank follows Group targets. Monitoring and actions to mitigate financed emissions are in place; Executive Steering Committee approval planned for 05.02.2025.
  - Operational target: carbon-neutral Scope 1–2 by 2030 (absolute, not science-based); 2024 market-based Scope 1–2 emissions were 6,644 tCO2e; electricity largely green; real estate and fleet intensity reduction planning to be prepared in 2025.
  - Action packages: portfolio-level (climate targeting and scaling green lending) and operational (energy efficiency and renewables). Operational measures include green electricity procurement, lighting and boiler upgrades, HVAC optimization, insulation, and solar installations.
- GHG emissions and financed emissions:
  - Methodology aligned with group reporting; OTP Bank 2024 Scope 1 = 5,565 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based = 1,079 tCO2e (total 6,644 tCO2e).
  - Significant Scope 3 (Category 15 – Investments) financed emissions were 24.836 MtCO2e in 2024 (-1% vs. 2023); 2030 target 16.855 MtCO2e (~-5.5% p.a.). PCAF-based breakdown by asset class provided; financed Scope 1–2 excluding sovereigns is the key indicator for climate targeting.
- Carbon credits and removals:
  - Purchased 7,000 tCO2e VCS-verified credits in 2024 covering Scope 1–2; project is the Saint Nikola Wind Farm in Bulgaria. Plans to complement offsets with a “habitat restoration certificate.”
  - Biodiversity and engagement initiative with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400 ha Budakeszi Wildlife Garden for ecosystem services, adaptation research, and employee engagement; no internal carbon pricing applied.
- ESG risk management and reporting: Group-wide ESG risk management foundations and environmental reporting policy apply at the individual bank level; further details referenced to the Group Sustainability Report.
- Social information (Own workforce):
  - Material topics: gender equality and equal pay; diversity; employment and inclusion of people with disabilities; training and skills development; health and safety; work-life balance; measures against workplace violence and harassment.
  - Own workforce includes employees and certain non-employee workers; practices primarily focus on employees; headcount of 10,820 employees.
text:
2. Climate change and environment  
Climate Change: Mitigation of Climate Change –Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities  
The impact of OTP Bank arises from direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating climate 
change. The direct emissions from operations and indirect emissions from energy consumption (Scope 1 -2) 
are relatively small. However, the indirect emissi ons associated with OTP Bank's loan portfolio (Scope 3) 
exceed Scope 1 -2 emissions by several orders of magnitude.  
In addition to emissions, the exemplary and awareness -raising impact that can be represented through its 
practices is also significant, considering the Bank's wide customer base.  
Expanding green lending to facilitate climate change mitigation represents a significant business opportunity 
for the Bank.  
It is significant for OTP Bank's lending activities because, in relation to climate change mitigation, a transition 
risk arises for a portion of its customer base, which indirectly poses a risk to the Bank as well. The extent of 
this risk is estimated thro ugh stress testing in relation to the corporate portfolio.  
Mitigating climate change as a material  topic at OTP Bank  
The Bank Group aims to facilitate climate change mitigation by reducing emissions associated with its lending 
and own operations, a goal supported by OTP Bank as well. At the end of 2024, a climate target was set for 
the loan portfolio, and the OTP Group a lso aims to play a leading financing role in the green and just transition 
in the long term. In the ESG strategy, a KPI has been set for green lending for the period up to 2025: OTP 
plans to build a green loan portfolio of HUF 1 ,500 billion by 2025. The po rtfolio is continuously growing, with 
the OTP Group's balance sheet green exposure amounting to HUF 1 ,027 billion at the end of 2024.  
The green lending targets are currently linked to the EU Taxonomy's mitigation and adaptation goals. The key 
sectors for green lending in the group's portfolio are: energy (renewable energy production, distribution, 
storage, and related lending goals), rea l-estate (construction, purchase, and sale of green properties, as well 
as financing renovations that result in significant building energy improvements), and transportation (electro -
mobility).  
In terms of green lending, the Bank strives to take advantage of regulatory incentives.  
The Bank continuously strives to reduce its Scope 1 -2 emissions. In addition to efficiency -enhancing actions, 
the use of green electric energy plays a significant role.  
OTP Bank has incorporated ESG risks into its risk management policies and procedures at the group level, 
enabling the identification and management of these risks to minimize emerging credit, reputational, regulatory, 
and legal risks. The management of ESG  risks is integrated into various levels of the risk ecosystem. Since 
2021, the Bank has been applying its ESG risk management framework in corporate lending to address the 
credit risk aspect of ESG risks.  
Risks arising from the Bank's own operations are managed within the framework of operational risks. The 
assessment of these risks is carried out through the Annual Group -level Risk and Control Self -Assessment 
and scenario analysis, based on the results of which risk mitigation actions are determined.  
Climate Change: Adaptation to Climate Change –Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities  
OTP Bank's lending practices impact adaptation, either by facilitating (expecting or supporting with favorable 
conditions), hindering, or remaining neutral towards customers' adaptation efforts. The necessity for adaptation 
is strongly required in several sectors within the portfolio (e.g., housing loans, agriculture, real -estate, 
construction sectors).  
The Bank strives to utilize the business opportunities arising from lending that facilitates adaptation to climate 
change.  
The physical risks associated with lending activities, as well as some of the transition risks (investments 
necessary for adaptation), are also related to this.  
Managing climate change adaptation as a material topic at OTP Bank  
The Bank strives to support adaptation to climate change through green lending. Risk management is 
conducted within the framework of ESG risk management.   MANAGEMENT REPORT (STAND -ALONE ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  67 Climate Change: Energy –Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities  
Through the financing of energy -intensive industries, the Bank influences the environmental impact of its 
clients' activities. By providing loans that encourage the use of renewable, carbon -free, and transitionally green 
energy sources, the Bank significan tly contributes to mitigating this impact. These goals represent a substantial 
proportion of green loans, and financing in these sectors is also significant.  
Similar to climate change mitigation and adaptation, business opportunities arise within green lending, where 
expanding the use of renewable and green -certified energy sources plays a significant role.  
Financing energy -intensive and fossil fuel -using companies poses credit and reputational risks for OTP Bank.  
Managing energy as a material topic at OTP Bank  
The Bank addresses this topic through the methods and tools presented in the previous two topics.  
30.23% of the Bank's green loan portfolio finances renewable energy.  
Water and Marine Resources: Water Withdrawal –Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities  
In OTP Bank's corporate loan portfolio, the presence of sectors with high water withdrawal is significant. To 
better understand the impacts, it is necessary to explore the practices employed by these companies.  
Financial risk primarily arises in relation to those clients who are unable to adequately manage changing or 
existing environmental expectations (e.g., tightening regulations, shifting consumer preferences, fines), or 
whose activities face difficulties in ensuring water supply. A deeper understanding of the risk requires further 
analysis.  
Managing water withdrawal is a material topic at OTP Bank  
The minimum expectations imposed and monitored by the Bank towards its clients include compliance with 
relevant environmental and social laws and regulations, as well as possessing the necessary permits and 
authorizations for their operations. Understandin g clients' practices beyond these requirements is ongoing 
alongside the evolving and strengthening regulatory expectations, based on which expectations promoting 
responsible behavior can be formulated.  
There is an opportunity to finance these goals within green lending. The Banking Group's minimum expectation 
for its clients, which is monitored, is compliance with relevant environmental and social laws and regulations, 
as well as possessing the necessary  permits and authorizations for their operations. Understanding clients' 
practices beyond these requirements is ongoing, in parallel with the evolving and strengthening regulatory 
expectations. Based on this, expectations that encourage responsible behavio r can be formulated.  
 
Risk management is conducted within the framework of ESG risk management.  
Biodiversity and ecosystems: Direct impact drivers of biodiversity loss  –impacts, risks, and 
opportunities  
The presence of sectors potentially having a negative impact on biodiversity and ecosystems is significant in 
OTP Bank's corporate loan portfolio. The Bank indirectly influences the extent of these impacts through its 
financing conditions and can also enco urage positive impacts. A more precise understanding of these impacts 
requires uncovering the practices employed by the companies.  
Managing direct impact drivers of biodiversity loss as a material topic at OTP Bank  
The minimum expectations imposed and monitored by the Bank towards its clients include compliance with 
relevant environmental and social laws and regulations, as well as possessing the necessary permits and 
authorizations for their operations (currently, there are significantly fewer requirements related to biodiversity 
compared to water). Understanding clients' practices beyond these requirements is ongoing alongside the 
evolving and strengthenin g regulatory expectations, based on which expectations promoting responsible 
behavior can be formulated.    MANAGEMENT REPORT (STAND -ALONE ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  68 ESRS E1 -2, E3 -1, E4 -2: Policies  
The OTP Group has a Group Credit Risk Policy and a Corporate Lending Policy / Operational Lending Limits 
and Guidelines, which also apply to OTP Bank. A detailed description of the policies can be found in subsection 
2.2. Climate change and environment – Policies in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
OTP Bank does not have a policy on water and biodiversity and ecosystems. The development of policies on 
water and biodiversity and ecosystems should be preceded by a deeper analysis of the risks involved in these 
two areas.  
In addition, the OTP Group’s Code of Ethics declares the Group's commitment to environmental sustainability 
and environmental values (see Governa nce Information ). 
ESRS E1 -4, E3 -3, E4 -4, E1 -9: Targets  
OTP Bank also contributes to the Group's two main climate change targets: GHG emission reduction target 
concerning the portfolio defined under climate targeting, and the green lending  target11. The content of these 
is briefly described below.  
Climate targeting  
In line with regulatory requirements, a plan to reduce the OTP Group's financed GHG emissions was defined 
in 2024. The plan sets targets to be achieved by 2030, based on the International Energy Agency's (IEA) Net 
Zero 2050 (NZE 2050) scenarios and national decarbonisation plans, and takes into account the current 
portfolio composition of OTP Group. OTP Bank foll ows the targets set by the Group, which are described in 
detail in subsection 2.2. Climate and Environment – Targets in the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
Actions to reduce financed emissions  
The OTP Group continuously monitors progress towards the 2030 climate target, taking into account whether 
external conditions allow the target to be met.  
In order to achieve its target, the OTP Group has set actions to reduce its financed emissions, which are also 
being followed by OTP Bank. A detailed description of the actions can be found in subsection 2.2. Climate 
change and environment – Actions to mit igate financed emissions of the OTP Group Sustainability Report.  
Approval of the climate target document by the Executive Steering Committee is planned for 05.02.2025.  
Green lending target  
OTP Bank also contributes to the OTP Group's goal, declared in its ESG strategy in 2021 and unchanged 
since then, to be a regional leader in financing a fair and gradual transition to a low -carbon economy and 
building a sustainable future through responsib le solutions12. The targets of the Banking Group are presented 
in detail in subsection 2.2. Climate change and environment – Green lending target in the OTP Group 
Sustainability Report.  
Further purposes  
In its ESG strategy for 2021, OTP Bank has set a target of achieving carbon -neutral operation by 2030. This 
absolute value target covers Scope 1 -2 emissions, and a related target of 0 tCO 2e, net zero emission is fixed, 
without identifying a base year. Net zero emissions is the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions where 
possible and the neutralisation of non -avoidable emissions through carbon dioxide removal. The target is not 
based on scientific evidence, OTP Bank's relevant departments were involved in its dev elopment. OTP Bank’s 
Scope 1 -2 market -based emissions in 2024 were 6,644 tCO 2e13. In terms of electricity, OTP Bank uses mostly 
green energy, with around three quarters of emissions coming from natural gas usage and vehicle fuel 
consumption. Preparation of the Bank's emissions intensity reduction plan for real -estate and fleet has sta rted, 
and an ESG Committee decision has been taken to prepare it in 2025.

No base year has been identified for the target, and green exposures in the stock  are measured from 2022 onwards.
