INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  170 Among others, we used:  
• ESG assessments and questionnaires: Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s.  
• Residential TRI*M Index research (Cross -country brand and satisfaction international, nationally 
representative52 residential research), which measured brand, satisfaction, and loyalty.  
• Employee engagement surveys, particularly OTP Group's53 2023 engagement measurement, 
which included 28,990 responses.  
• Specifically for OTP Group's materiality assessment, we sought opinions through an online 
stakeholder questionnaire from civil organizations and universities; authorities, supervisory 
authorities and public administration; financial analysts and stock exchanges; the media; and 
employee representatives. Based on  the feedback received, one topic was included in the list of 
material topics (employees: work -life balance), as more than a third of the respondents rated it as 
material. Regarding impact materiality, all stakeholders received the same questionnaire. We a lso 
sought the opinions of financial analysts and stock exchange stakeholders from a financial 
materiality perspective. The questionnaire primarily contained multiple -choice questions, but there 
was also the opportunity to raise additional potentially mate rial topics and, in the case of one 
question, to provide an open -ended response. Participants were informed about the background 
information needed to complete the questionnaire and the purpose of the questionnaire.  
Stakeholders specifically affected by pollution and resource use and the circular economy were not consulted.

title: Identification and Evaluation of Financial Risks and Opportunities
heading: Identification and Evaluation of Financial Risks and Opportunities
start_phrase: The identification of financial risks and opportunities related to sustainability topics was the result of an iterative process.
summary:
- Scope: Part of OTP Group’s 2024 Integrated Annual Report outlining stakeholder engagement, materiality, and the identification/evaluation of sustainability-related financial risks and opportunities.
- Stakeholder inputs used: ESG ratings/questionnaires (Sustainalytics, MSCI, Moody’s); Residential TRI*M brand/satisfaction research; 2023 employee engagement survey (28,990 responses); an online stakeholder questionnaire targeting civil society, academia, authorities/supervisors/public administration, financial analysts/stock exchanges, media, and employee representatives.
- Materiality outcome: “Employees: work-life balance” added as a material topic based on stakeholder feedback; the impact-materiality questionnaire was standardized across stakeholder groups with options for open-ended input; stakeholders directly affected by pollution, resource use, and circular economy were not consulted.
- Financial risks/opportunities identification process: Iterative approach starting from ESRS topics, inputs used for impact materiality, SASB financial sector standards, and ESG rating topics; no additional topics emerged from SASB/ESG ratings.
- Shortlisting and time horizons: Workshops with OTP Bank experts determined relevant topics and assessed their short-, medium-, and long-term relevance.
- Materiality thresholds: No universal financial materiality threshold; thresholds derived from source documents or set case-by-case due to varied financial impacts.
- Risk governance approach: ESG risks integrated holistically into existing risk types (loan, country, counterparty, market, liquidity, operational, compliance) rather than treated as a standalone risk.
- Sources of financial risks/opportunities:
  - Opportunities aligned with ESG strategy and annual plans.
  - Lending-related sustainability risks: Group-wide Climate & Environmental (C&E) Risk Materiality Assessment initiated in 2024 per EBA; pending results substituted with a 2023 climate change stress test and NACE-based income analysis; supplemented by subsidiary Environmental Risk Materiality Assessments.
  - Operational risks: Identified via annual group-level RCSA; sustainability-attributable operational risks mapped to sustainability topics.
- Evaluation method: Risks and opportunities assessed on a three-level scale for magnitude and likelihood; items rated medium/large or large/large deemed material.
- Climate-related specifics:
  - Lending transition/physical risks assessed via the 2023 group climate stress test (using NGFS scenarios) and select subsidiary C&E assessments (Bulgarian and Croatian examples).
  - Own-operations risks evaluated via the 2023 RCSA: climate-related hazards (mainly physical and supply chain) did not meet materiality thresholds; results inform operational risk capital requirements and are reviewed by the Group Operational Risk Management Committee.
  - Subsidiary insights: Croatian assessment classed operational physical risks as low–medium (short/medium term) and medium (long term), not material; Bulgarian analysis indicated moderate exposure.
- Footnotes/coverage notes: Residential survey urban-only in Moldova, Ukraine, Uzbekistan; Uzbek employee opinion process being phased in; Russian subsidiary used a different engagement platform; NGFS referenced for climate scenarios.
text:
Identification and Evaluation of Financial Risks and Opportunities   
The identification of financial risks and opportunities related to sustainability topics was the result of an iterative 
process.  
As a starting point for identifying financial risks and opportunities (long list):  
• We used the topics included in ESRS,  
• Supplemented with inputs also used for impact materiality,  
• SASB standards for the financial sector, and  
• ESG rating topics.  
Based on the latter two inputs, no new topics needed to be added.  
The sustainability topics where relevant risks or opportunities might arise for OTP Group (short list) were 
identified in workshops and subsequent consultations with the involvement of OTP Bank's experts. Participants 
considered whether the risks and oppor tunities were relevant in the short, medium, or long term.  
The deeper exploration and evaluation of risks and opportunities began for the relevant topics. The Banking 
Group does not use a threshold applicable to all areas for financial materiality. OTP Group experts did not 
consider it justified or practical to ap ply such a threshold, partly because different risks and opportunities can 
have different financial impacts. Therefore, during the evaluation we applied the threshold values (or derived 
conclusions) from the documents used for the evaluation, and if these were not available, we determined the 
threshold value during the materiality assessment.  
OTP Group has detailed risk management policies and systems covering all types of risks (loan, country, 
counterparty, market, liquidity, operational, compliance), including ESG risk management, the practice of which 
is continuously evolving. OTP Group take s a holistic approach to ESG risks and ESG factors, integrating them 
into the risk management frameworks of the main risk types, i.e. treating ESG risk as a risk type rather than a 
stand -alone risk type. Sustainability risks are considered together with ot her risks.  
Financial risks and opportunities arising from sustainability topics can originate from three main sources, which 
were examined as follows:  
• For opportunities, the ESG strategy and annual plans are decisive, as the strategy focuses on 
exploiting material opportunities.  
 
52 Except for Moldova, Ukraine and Uzbekistan, where the survey was conducted based on an urban sample. 
53 The process of understanding the opinions of the employees of the Uzbek subsidiary will be introduced gradually, according to  a unique schedule. In 
the Russian subsidiary, the e ngagement survey  was carried out on a different platform and based on a list of questions. 
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  171 • The implementation of the Climate & Environmental (C&E) Risk Materiality Assessment for the 
group -level assessment of sustainability risks related to lending activities started in 2024, in line 
with the European Banking Authority (EBA) requirements. The result s of this assessment were not 
available at the time of the materiality assessment and the start of this reporting. Therefore, as an 
alternative solution for evaluating these risks, we analysed the results of the climate change stress 
test and the income fr om interest and net fees and commissions based on activities broken up by 
NACE codes. The matching of risks with activities was done in the same way as applied for impact 
materiality. Another source of information was the Environmental Risk Materiality Ass essment 
available at some subsidiaries.  
• Other topics representing relevant risks fall into the category of operational risks. OTP Group 
conducts an annual group -level Risk and Control Self -Assessment (RCSA) to identify operational 
risks. During the process, departments identify operational risks  in their processes, their likelihood 
of occurrence in different cases, and link risk mitigation mechanisms, i.e., control functions and 
activities, to the identified operational risks. Among the risks identified in this process, those 
attributable to sust ainability reasons were assigned to sustainability topics.  
We evaluated relevant risks and opportunities on a 3 -level scale (large, medium, small) based on (1) their 
potential magnitude and (2) their likelihood. We considered medium/large and large/large risks and 
opportunities as material.

title: Additional information to the assessment of climate change related topics
heading: Additional information to the assessment of climate change related topics:
start_phrase: In line with the general procedure applied during the identification and evaluation of impacts, the identification of risks and opportunities was also based on activities.
summary:
- OTP Group began a Climate & Environmental (C&E) Risk Materiality Assessment in 2024 to meet EBA requirements; because results were not yet available, the Group used a climate change stress test and analysis of income by NACE codes, plus selected subsidiary environmental risk assessments, to evaluate sustainability risks linked to lending.
- Operational risks relevant to sustainability were identified through the annual group-level Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA), which maps process risks, likelihoods, and controls; sustainability-attributable risks were assigned to related sustainability topics.
- Risks and opportunities were rated on a three-level scale for magnitude and likelihood, with materiality defined for medium/large and large/large combinations.
- Transition and physical risks for lending were assessed using the 2023 group climate stress test based on NGFS scenarios; Bulgarian and Croatian subsidiaries’ C&E Risk Materiality Assessments were used as additional inputs.
- For own operations, the 2023 RCSA formed the basis for analyzing operational risks; climate-related hazards mainly fell under physical risks (including supply chain), were identified without a predefined hazard/asset list, and did not meet the materiality threshold. RCSA results inform operational risk capital requirements and indicate short-term risks, with trends highlighting medium/long-term outlooks.
- Subsidiary assessments: Croatia classified operational risks from extreme weather as low–medium in the short/medium term and medium in the long term (not material by its criteria); Bulgaria indicated moderate exposure.
- The reviewed documents did not identify assets or activities incompatible with a climate-neutral transition; climate-related risks were deemed manageable for the Group.
- Financial opportunities were guided by the ESG strategy and annual plans, notably expanding the green loan portfolio through 2025.
- Material climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities are disclosed under ESRS SBM-3.
- Validation and governance: a multi-round internal review incorporated stakeholder feedback; the ESG Sub-Committee approved the material list (after one modification) by majority, the ESG Committee approved it unanimously, and outcomes were reported to the Board of Directors via ESG Committee briefings.
text:
Additional information to the assessment of climate change related topics:  
In line with the general procedure applied during the identification and evaluation of impacts, the identification 
of risks and opportunities was also based on activities.  
Regarding the assessment of transition and physical risks  related to lending activities:  
• OTP Group's 2023 group -level climate change stress test evaluated the risks as presented in the 
@Stress -test (For long -term impacts, the use of NGFS54 climate scenarios in the banking sector is the 
generally accepted and mostly alternative -free approach.)  
• The group -level stress test provided suitable basis for the evaluation, while some subsidiaries had 
their own environmental risk materiality assessments ( C&E Risk Materiality Assessment) , which cover 
other credit risks, among which we considered the assessments of the Bulgarian and Croatian 
subsidiaries as examples.  
With regards to the assessment of financial risks related to own operations, the following was analysed:  
• The annual group -level Risk and Control Self -Assessment (RCSA) 2023 provided the basis for the 
analysis of operational risks. During the annual self -assessment process, departments identify 
operational risks in their processes, their likelihood of occurren ce in different cases, and link risk 
mitigation mechanisms to the identified operational risks. The annual RCSA results and their detailed 
evaluation were submitted to the Group Operational Risk Management Committee, and these results 
are also part of the calculation of operational risk management capital requirements. The RCSA 
measures the risks for the next year (short term), with the risk trend indicating medium and long -term 
risks. Climate -related hazards identified during the evaluation fell into the c ategory of physical risks, 
and the risk of events occurring in the supply chain was also identified. Participants could identify any 
climate -related hazard or risk, and no prior exclusion of climate -related risks was made. Based on the 
applied methodology,  similar to other non -climate -related risks, departments did not evaluate risks 
using a predefined hazard list and asset list. Climate change -related risks did not reach the materiality 
threshold in the RCSA evaluation.  
• The Climate & Environmental Risk Materiality Assessment of the Bulgarian and Croatian subsidiary 
bank also examined operational risks, among other things, and the results were taken into account. 
The Croatian document classified the operational risks mainl y due to extreme weather events (physical 
risk) as low -medium risk in the short to medium term and medium risk in the long term (which is not a 
material risk level according to the document's own classification). The Bulgarian analysis indicated 
moderate e xposure.  
 
54 The Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System.

INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  172 The above documents did not address the identification of assets and business activities that are incompatible 
with the transition to a climate -neutral economy or those requiring significant effort for this transition. The risks 
identified in relation to c limate change were considered manageable for OTP Group.  
For financial opportunities , we considered the ESG strategy (@Strategy ) and annual plans as decisive, as 
the strategy focuses on exploiting material opportunities. Expanding the green loan portfolio is included as a 
financial opportunity in the ESG strategy. The strategy covered the time period up to 2025 at the time of the 
analysis.  
The material impacts, risks, and opportunities related to climate change are presented in the @ESRS SBM -3 
disclosure.

title: Validation of the evaluation and approval
heading: Validation of the evaluation and approval
start_phrase: The evaluation of impacts, risks, and opportunities was followed by a multi -round internal review.
summary:
- Scope: Extract from OTP Group’s 2024 Integrated Annual Report (Management Report) presenting ESRS SBM-3 disclosure on material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities, focused on climate change mitigation and adaptation.

- Materiality process and governance:
  - Evaluation underwent multi-round internal review, with stakeholder feedback from Hungarian and foreign subsidiaries.
  - ESG Sub-Committee approved the final list by majority after one modification; ESG Committee approved unanimously; the Committee Chair sits on the Board.
  - Results were reported to the Board of Directors via ESG Committee quarterly agendas.

- Identification and risk posture:
  - Earlier documents did not identify assets/activities incompatible with a climate-neutral transition or those needing significant transition effort.
  - Climate-related risks were deemed manageable for OTP Group.

- Strategy and opportunities:
  - ESG strategy and annual plans guide financial opportunities; expansion of green lending is a key opportunity.
  - Strategy time horizon extends to 2025; OTP’s balance sheet green exposure is increasing.

- Climate change mitigation (E1):
  - Impacts: OTP’s Scope 3 emissions (especially from the loan portfolio and asset managers) vastly exceed Scope 1–2; Scope 1–2 are relatively small per entity but significant in aggregate. Some smaller group members in agriculture, food, and real estate have relatively higher direct emissions.
  - Management: A loan portfolio decarbonization/transition plan was prepared by end-2024; KPI for green lending set through 2025; Scope 1–2 reductions via efficiency and green electricity.
  - Positive impact: Financial products and OTP’s broad customer reach foster mitigation and awareness.
  - Opportunity: Grow green lending in corporate and retail mortgages (no active green lending per OTP standards in Ukraine).
  - Risk: Client transition risks indirectly affect OTP; assessed via corporate portfolio stress testing and managed within ESG risk management.

- Climate change adaptation (E1):
  - Impacts: Lending can facilitate, hinder, or be neutral to clients’ adaptation; high adaptation needs in mortgages, agriculture, real estate, and construction.
  - Management: Promote adaptation through green lending; risks handled within ESG risk management.
  - Opportunity: Expand lending that supports adaptation.
  - Risks: Physical risks tied to lending exposure and certain transition risks from necessary adaptation investments.

- Coverage and horizons: Impacts, risks, and opportunities are considered across the value chain (upstream, OTP Group, downstream) and over short, medium, and long terms.
text:
Validation of the evaluation and approval  
The evaluation of impacts, risks, and opportunities was followed by a multi -round internal review. As part of 
this, the evaluation of impacts rated below but close to the materiality threshold was reviewed based on 
stakeholder feedback. Representatives of Hungarian subsidiaries and foreign subsidiary banks could also 
provide feedback on the materiality assessment.  
The ESG Sub -Committee discussed the list of material impacts, risks, and opportunities and, after one 
modification, approved it by majority decision in accordance with the Sub -Committee's operating rules.  
The ESG Committee discussed and approved the results of the materiality assessment. A unanimous decision 
was required for approval in accordance with the Committee's operating rules. The Chairman of the ESG 
Committee is a member of the Board of Directors.  
The results of the materiality analysis were included in the Board of Directors' briefing on the agenda items of 
the ESG Committee's quarterly meetings.

title: OTP Group’s Material Sustainability Impacts, risks and opportunities
heading: ESRS SBM -3 OTP Group’s Material Sustainability Impacts, risks and opportunities
start_phrase: OTP Group's impact stems from direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, exacerbating climate change.
summary:
- Scope and framework: The excerpt outlines OTP Group’s material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities across its value chain and time horizons, structured under ESRS SBM-3 and linked to ESRS 2 IRO-2. It identifies where impacts occur (upstream, own operations, downstream) and their relevance in the short, medium, and long term.

- E1 Climate change mitigation and adaptation:
  - Mitigation: The Group’s most material environmental impact is GHG emissions from financed activities (Scope 3) far exceeding operational emissions (Scopes 1–2). A loan-portfolio decarbonization plan was prepared by end-2024; a green lending KPI runs to 2025; green balance sheet exposure is growing; green electricity and efficiency reduce Scopes 1–2. Material risks stem from client transition risks assessed via stress testing and managed within ESG risk management. Opportunities center on expanding green lending (excluding Ukraine).
  - Adaptation: Lending can facilitate client adaptation in mortgages, agriculture, real estate, and construction; managed within ESG risk frameworks. Opportunities in adaptation finance; risks include physical and related transition needs.

- Energy: Negative impact via financing energy-intensive sectors; positive impact and opportunity via financing renewables and energy efficiency; credit and reputational risks when financing fossil and energy-intensive clients.

- E3 Water and marine resources (water withdrawal): Significant exposure to high-withdrawal sectors in the corporate portfolio; minimum client expectations include legal compliance and permits, with deeper practice assessments evolving alongside regulation. Positive impact through green lending; risks if clients fail to meet tightening standards or secure water availability.

- E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Exposure to sectors with potential negative biodiversity impacts; current expectations focus on compliance due to fewer biodiversity-specific rules, with ongoing work to understand client practices and articulate responsible expectations. No significant impacts identified for land degradation/desertification/soil sealing. Potential to encourage positive outcomes via financing conditions.

- S1 Own workforce (43,118 employees):
  - Work-life balance: Benefits, flexibility, leave, and well-being programs generate positive impacts; potential negatives if needs not addressed.
  - Health and safety: Stress is a key risk; OHS programs, preventive health checks, and stress management in place.
  - Gender equality and equal pay: Strategy and diversity policies; generally minimal pay gaps in same roles, but women underrepresented at senior levels and some subsidiaries show larger gaps.
  - Training and skills: Broad training portfolio aligned with evaluations; risk of unequal access if not well managed.
  - Inclusion of persons with disabilities: Non-discrimination in place, but supportive measures limited and employment share low.
  - Measures against violence/harassment: Ethics framework active; potential risk persists.
  - Diversity: Anti-discrimination stance, with room to improve practical implementation.

- S4 Consumers and end-users (financial services entities):
  - Information security and data protection (incl. cybersecurity): Robust systems, training, and anti-fraud support produce positive impacts, though incidents can still cause customer losses; significant legal, financial, and reputational risk if breaches occur.
  - Access to quality information: Regulated communications, education tools, and simplification efforts support informed decisions, with residual gaps due to product complexity.
  - Access to financial products and services: Digitalization to improve accessibility, including for disadvantaged areas; support for state-backed mortgage schemes; access improving but not comprehensive.

- G1 Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture, compliance, AML/CFT: Code of Ethics, ethics reporting, annual training, AML/CFT training and whistleblowing; positive impacts yet non-compliances can occur; legal, reputational, liquidity, and correspondent banking risks highlighted.
  - Corruption and bribery: Anti-corruption training, contractual clauses (expanding groupwide), and risk assessments; potential abuses cannot be fully eliminated.

- ESG risk, resilience, and financial impacts:
  - No dedicated provisions or capital buffers for ESG risks; impairments recognized in Slovenia and Bulgaria under ECB Novel Risk Recommendation, reflected in IFRS 9 ECL; additional climate risk capital needs not material.
  - ESG factors to enter rating models in 2025; operational risk losses flagged for ESG where relevant; no significant ESG-related losses in 2024; analysis and estimation of expected financial impacts planned for 2025.
  - Climate stress testing performed; no biodiversity resilience assessment due to non-financial materiality; ongoing monitoring of market and regulatory changes.

- Sanctions supplement: Operations subject to UN, EU, UK, US sanctions and Russian countersanctions; elevated exposure to Russia-related measures. Risks include inability to unwind sanctioned relationships in time, fines, license restrictions, reputational damage, and financial consequences; litigation/investigation risks acknowledged.

- Reporting policy and entity-specific disclosures:
  - Material topics and data points selected using EFRAG ID 177 guidance; voluntary data reported where feasible; phased ESRS adoption applied.
  - For own operations, only E1 climate mitigation is impact-material among environmental topics; other E1/E3/E4 not considered relevant for own operations.
  - S4 impacts are material specifically for clients; related data points reported for these client segments.
  - Entity-specific disclosures in scope: to be developed for water withdrawal and biodiversity impact drivers in the value chain; current disclosures cover information security and data protection, access to quality information, access to financial products and services, and corporate culture/compliance/AML.

title: Sanctions Supplement
heading: Sanctions Supplement: OTP Group’s operations are affected by various anti -corruption laws, sanctions enacted and applied by the UN, the UK and the EU, as well as the United States.
start_phrase: In addition, OTP Group’s operations in Russia are subject to various Russia n countersanctions.
summary:
- The report outlines OTP Group’s exposure to and compliance with international anti-corruption laws and sanctions regimes from the UN, UK, EU, and US, as well as Russian countersanctions affecting its Russian operations.
- It highlights restrictions on dealings with sanctioned countries, entities, and individuals, emphasizing heightened risk related to sanctions on Russia, Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine, and targeted Russian/Ukrainian parties, including owned/controlled entities.
- The Group notes potential exposure if customers become sanctioned and services are not ceased within permitted wind-down periods, acknowledging that evolving sanctions could have a material impact on operations.
- It details risks of investigations and litigation for alleged sanctions or anti-corruption breaches, including fines, activity restrictions, license revocation, reputational damage, and broader financial consequences.
- OTP Group identifies entity-specific disclosures for material topics: water withdrawal (value chain; disclosure under development), direct drivers of biodiversity loss (value chain; disclosure under development), information security and data protection, access to quality information, access to financial products and services, and corporate culture/compliance/anti-money laundering.
- Under ESRS 2 IRO-2, the Group reports on disclosure requirements tied to material sub-topics, using EFRAG ID 177 to link topics and define data points; it voluntarily reports feasible data points and applies phased ESRS options where relevant.
- For environmental topics, only climate change mitigation is considered materially impactful for the Group’s own operations; other E1, E3 (water and marine), and E4 (biodiversity and ecosystems) data points are deemed not relevant to own operations.
- S4 (Consumers and End-users) impacts and risks are material for specific client segments within Group banks, and the report includes the corresponding data points for these clients.
text:
Sanctions Supplement: OTP Group’s operations are affected by various anti -corruption laws, sanctions 
enacted and applied by the UN, the UK and the EU, as well as the United States. In addition, OTP Group’s 
operations in Russia are subject to various Russia n countersanctions. In the course of its business activities, 
OTP Group may come into contact with organizations whose employees are considered public officials.  
Applicable sanctions may restrict OTP Group’s dealings with certain sanctioned countries, individuals and 
organizations. OTP Group is particularly exposed to risks related to economic sanctions imposed by the United 
States, the EU and the United Kingdom ag ainst Russia and the Russian -occupied territories of Ukraine, as 
well as certain targeted Russian and Ukrainian organizations and individuals, as well as entities owned or 
controlled by such targeted organizations and individuals.  
The imposition of any current or future sanctions may result in OTP Group’s existing or future customers being 
subject to sanctions, directly or indirectly. If OTP Group is unable to cease providing services to sanctioned 
parties within the permitted wind -down period (if any) and such customers continue to be subject to sanctions 
and/or are included in sanction lists, this may also expose OTP Group to the risk of being subject to sanctions. 
OTP Group cannot provide assurances that current or future sanction s targeting Russia, Russian companies 
and associated companies will not have a material impact on OTP Group’s operations.  
Litigation or investigations related to alleged or suspected violations of anti -corruption laws and sanctions may 
result in OTP Group being fined, restricted in its activities, revoked in its licenses, damaged in its reputation, 
and other adverse consequen ces on its activities and financial consequences. Additionally, violations of anti -
corruption laws and sanctions regulations may result in financial disadvantage.  
OTP Group also applies entity -specific disclosures  to inform about the impacts of the following material 
topics:  
• Water withdrawal is a material topic concerning the value chain, for which entity -specific disclosure 
will be developed later  
• Direct impact drivers of biodiversity loss is a material topic concerning the value chain, for which entity -
specific disclosure will be developed later  
• Information security and data protection  
• Access to (quality) information  
• Access to financial products and services  
• Corporate culture, compliance, anti -money laundering

title: Disclosure Requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement and general reporting policy
heading: 1.5. Disclosure Requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability statement and general reporting policy
start_phrase: Among the disclosure requirements and data points in the thematic standards of ESRS, we report those that are related to the material sub -topics for OTP Group.
summary:
- Sanctions and anti-corruption exposure: OTP Group’s operations are affected by UN, UK, EU, and US sanctions and Russian countersanctions. The Group faces risks if customers become sanctioned, if wind-downs cannot be executed in time, and from potential investigations, fines, license impacts, reputational damage, and financial losses.
- Material topics and entity-specific disclosures: Current focus includes information security/data protection, access to information, access to financial products/services, and corporate culture/compliance/AML. Water withdrawal and biodiversity-loss drivers are material in the value chain; entity-specific disclosures for these will be developed later.
- ESRS reporting approach (ESRS 2 IRO-2): Reporting is limited to material sub-topics, mapped using EFRAG ID 177. Voluntary data points are provided when feasible; phased-in options are used where allowed. For own operations, only climate change mitigation is material; other E1 topics, E3 (water), and E4 (biodiversity) are not considered material for own operations. S4 (consumers/end-users) is material for certain client segments, with related data reported.
- Policies, actions, and targets: Disclosures cover the parent and specified subsidiaries across multiple countries; OTP Bank Romania (sold mid-year) is excluded. Asset managers are included where SFDR-linked climate information is relevant. For S1 (own workforce), entities with over 250 employees are covered. Where no policy/action/target exists, this is stated. Metrics aim for full coverage, with a threshold applied to ESRS S1-16 (compensation metrics); metrics are assured by the service provider, with no other external validation.
- Entity-specific disclosure methodology and definitions: Plans to develop entity-specific metrics for topics not covered by ESRS (notably S4 and, pending data, E3/E4). Definitions provided for operational control and business relationships. Associates/joint ventures are included beyond equity share when assessing value-chain impacts. Governance disclosures include board composition (gender, independence) and criteria. Country breakdown and total income are defined.
- Environmental strategy and progress: OTP seeks regional leadership in financing a fair, gradual low-carbon transition, expanding green loans and corporate bonds in 2024, enhancing risk management, and aiming to reduce operational footprint. A climate target-setting document establishes 2030 Scope 3 (Category 15) GHG targets in absolute and relative terms (not an ESRS E1-1 transition plan).
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - E1 Climate change: Own operations’ GHG emissions (negative impact); green financial products and internal practices (positive impacts/opportunities); transition and physical risks in the loan/investment portfolios.
  - E2 Water and marine resources: Portfolio exposure to high water-abstraction sectors (negative), opportunities via green lending, and water-dependency/compliance risks.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: Portfolio exposure to sectors harming biodiversity (negative) and potential to influence client behavior through expectations (positive).
- EU Taxonomy Regulation disclosures: Prepared per Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, reporting on exposures within prudential consolidation (CRR 575/2013). Confirms applicability under Articles 19a/29a and Article 8 disclosure obligations and reiterates OTP’s commitment to sustainable finance and social responsibility.
text:
5. Disclosure Requirements in ESRS covered by the undertaking’s sustainability 
statement and general reporting policy  
ESRS 2 IRO -2 
Among the disclosure requirements and data points in the thematic standards of ESRS, we report those that 
are related to the material sub -topics for OTP Group. To link material topics and disclosure requirements, we 
used the EFRAG ID 177 – Links between AR 16 and Disclosure requirements guideline, and the identification 
of data points was based on the interpretation of data point expectations.  
Data points  
We report voluntarily reportable data points if the required information can be produced without significant 
effort or if we have previously reported them. In several cases, we utilize the phased introduction option 
specified in the ESRS, and these data po ints are not included in the report.  
Regarding environmental topics, only Climate Change Mitigation is material – in terms of impact materiality – 
for our own operations. We do not consider data points related to other E1 (climate change) topics, E3 (water 
and marine resources), and E4 (biodi versity and ecosystems) topics relevant for our own operations.  
The material impacts and risks related to the S4 (Consumers and End -users) topic are specifically material for 
the clients and specific portion of clients of the (banks within the Group) (see @ESRS SBM -3). We report the 
related data points for these clients.

- OTP Group’s environmental strategy: aims to lead regionally in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy; expanded green loan and corporate bond portfolios in 2024; issued a climate target‑setting document for 2030 (Scope 3 category 15, absolute and intensity targets; not an ESRS E1‑1 transition plan); strengthened risk management; seeks to cut operational environmental footprint.

- Material environmental topics and impacts:
  - Climate (E1): own operations and portfolios contribute to direct/indirect GHG emissions (negative); opportunities through green financial products and internal practices that shape mindsets; portfolio financial risks from transition and physical climate risks; financial opportunities in green lending.
  - Water (E2): potential negative impact via financing high water withdrawal sectors; opportunities via green lending; portfolio risks from water dependency and environmental compliance.
  - Biodiversity (E4): potential negative impacts via funding biodiversity‑affecting sectors; potential positive leverage by setting client expectations for responsible behavior.

- EU Taxonomy Regulation disclosures:
  - Reporting aligned to Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; scope based on prudential consolidation under CRR 575/2013.
  - Discloses stock and flow metrics, transitional and enabling activities, and specialized vs general‑purpose lending.
  - Consolidated KPIs include exposures of subsidiaries, fund managers, and credit institutions.
  - Certain exposures excluded from mandatory KPIs: corporates not subject to Articles 19a/29a disclosures and non‑EU subsidiary banks; these are discussed in the green lending section.
  - Qualitative methodology and data details provided per Annex XI.
  - The Commission Notice (C/2024/6691) Appendix 2 table not published due to late issuance; to be included next year. Separate chapter covers asset manager KPIs (OTP Fund Management).

- Key performance indicators (GAR) and trends:
  - 2024 GAR stock improved:
    - Turnover‑based: 0.10% (vs 0.05% in 2023), HUF 30,365 million environmentally sustainable assets.
    - Capex‑based: 0.29% (vs 0.09% in 2023), HUF 82,911 million environmentally sustainable assets.
  - 2024 GAR flow increased to 0.13% (turnover) and 0.45% (capex).
  - KPI coverage remains ~65% of total assets; both GAR assets and total balance sheet grew by >13%.
  - Financial institutions: taxonomy‑eligible exposures reached ~2.5%; aligned ~0.10%, aided by broader taxonomy reporting availability.
  - Non‑financial corporates: taxonomy‑eligible exposures exceed 8.5% (turnover basis); aligned ratio above 3%.
  - Households: taxonomy‑eligible ratios ~28% overall; 57% for real‑estate‑secured exposures; ~37% for retail motor vehicle finance. Bank does not count these as aligned when only substantial contribution is met due to DNSH evidence gaps; household category interpreted as total gross exposure (EU and non‑EU) per 2024 Commission Notice.

- 2023 restatement for managed assets in GAR templates:
  - Turnover basis (Template 1, Row 55): total AUM +1,526,575 million HUF; taxonomy‑eligible +124,025 million HUF; aligned +9,337 million HUF.
  - Capex basis (Template 1, Row 55): total AUM +1,526,575 million HUF; taxonomy‑eligible +314,352 million HUF; aligned +14,882 million HUF.
  - As a result, 2023 consolidated sustainability data in this report are not comparable to last year’s publication; comparative GAR KPIs are still provided as required by Article 8.

- KPI coverage and exclusions snapshot (2024):
  - GAR stock coverage over total assets: 64.76%; assets excluded from numerator: 27.43%; assets excluded from denominator: 35.24%.
  - Additional KPIs: GAR flow coverage 58.52%; assets under management taxonomy‑aligned activities equal to 0.37% (turnover) and 0.68% (capex).
  - Fees and commissions and trading book KPIs will apply starting in 2026.

1.1. EU Taxonomy Regulation Disclosures  
Information to be disclosed by companies covered by Articles 19a or 29a of Directive 2013/34/EU of the 
European Parliament and of the Council (EU) 2020/852 on environmentally sustainable economic activities, 
based on the methodology set out in Commission D elegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178. For the credit 
institutions of OTP Group, the reporting is based on exposures and balance sheets corresponding to the scope 
of prudential consolidation according to Section 2 of Chapter 2 of Title II of Regulation (EU) N o 575/2013, as 
set out in Annex V, point 1 of the current Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 2021/2178.  
OTP Bank is committed to sustainable financing and social responsibility.  
Mandatory Disclosures  
The Taxonomy Regulation applies to financial market participants that make available financial products and 
undertakings which are subject to the obligation to publish a non -financial statement or a consolidated non -
financial statement pursuant to Article 19a or Article 29a of Directive No. 2013/34/EU of the European 
Parliament and of the Council, respectively (Article 1 (b) and (c) of Chapter I of (EU) 2020/852). Pursuant to 
Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation, any undertaking which is subject to an oblig ation to disclose non -
financial information pursuant to Article 19a or Article 29a of Directive No. 2013/34/EU shall include in its non -
financial statement or consolidated non -financial statement information on how and to what extent the 
 
62 This document defines a GHG target for 2030 in both absolute and relative terms, relating to category 15 of OTP Group's Scope  3 emissions, and 
identifies the main instruments to ensure the achievement of the target; however, it is not considered a transition plan acco rding to the ESRS E1 -1 
disclosure requirement.  
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  182 undertaking’s activities are associated with economic activities that qualify as environmentally sustainable 
under Articles 3 and 9 of (EU) 2020/852 Regulation. OTP Group report is based on the exposures and balance 
sheet according to the scope of prudenti al consolidation in accordance with Regulation (EU) No. 575/2013, 
Title II, Chapter 2, Section 2 for the types of assets and accounting portfolios specified in point 1.1.2 of Annex 
V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No. 2021/2178, including informat ion on stock and flows, on 
transitional and enabling activities, and on specialized and general purpose lending.  
The tables below present the consolidated information on OTP Group’s mandatory KPIs under Regulation 
(EU) No. 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation), which have been prepared using the template published in Annex 
VI of Regulation No. 2021/2178. The gross carrying amount is based on the reference date of 31. December 
2024.  
OTP Group discloses the relevant KPIs on a consolidated basis, considering the scope of prudential 
consolidation, in accordance with Annex V, point 1.1.1 of EU 2021/2178. Accordingly, the exposures of the 
various subsidiaries, including those of fund manag ers and credit institutions, are part of the consolidated credit 
institution KPIs.  
In regard to the publication of the table in Appendix 2 of the third Commission Notice of November 2024 
(C/2024/6691 Commission Notice), OTP Group has chosen not to publish it in this reporting year, due to the 
late publication of the Notice. The publicati on of the table will be taken into account by OTP Group in the next 
reporting year.  In the case of OTP Fund Management Ltd, the requirements for asset managers have been 
taken into account and the KPIs for asset managers is presented in a separate chapter.  
The calculation of the main KPI indicators has been based on the best understanding of the requirements set 
out in the Delegated Regulation and the KPIs have been set accordingly.  
In accordance with the legislation, the main KPI indicators are calculated as a proportion of total green assets, 
which is not equal to the Bank's total balance sheet. OTP Group's corporate loan portfolio is dominated by 
companies that are not subject to t he obligation to disclose non -financial information under Articles 19a or 29a 
of Directive 2013/34/EU. As the eligible and aligned exposures to these entities are not included in the 
mandatory disclosure, they are disclosed in the ( @green lending ) section of this report. Exposures to non -EU 
subsidiary banks as defined above are also not covered by the mandatory reporting and are excluded from 
the calculation of the KPIs.  
The qualitative disclosures required by Annex XI of the Delegated Regulation provide detailed information on 
the data and methodology used by the Bank.  
The main stock and flow KPI indicators of OTP Group show the following changes compared to the previous 
year:

Significant efforts in green financing lead to improvements in key KPIs. For taxonomy aligned stocks, 
compared to the same data last year, the KPI shows a significant increase on both a capex and turnover basis.  
On turnover basis, our taxonomy aligned exp osures increased from 0.05% to 0.10% and on a capex basis 
from 0.09% to 0.29% of GAR assets. The proportion of assets included in the calculation of the main KPIs 
within the total balance sheet remained broadly unchanged at around 65% . Both GAR assets and total bank 
balance sheet data increased by more than 13%.  
Taxonomy - eligible and aligned exposures to financial institutions improved severalfold, one of the main 
reasons being the wider availability of taxonomy reports for financial corporations. Taxonomy -eligible 
exposures reach 2.5%, while taxonomy -aligned exp osures reach 0.10%.  
Taxonomy -eligible exposures to non -financial corporates exceed 8.5% on a turnover basis and the taxonomy -
aligned ratio on turnover basis is above 3%.   
With respect to exposures to households, in case only the substantial contribution (SC) criterion is met, the 
Bank does not report these exposures as taxonomy -aligned exposures, given that it cannot currently 
demonstrate compliance with the DNSH conditions . 
In line with the interpretation of the third Commission Notice (C/2024/6691 Commission Notice) published in 
November 2024, the Bank interprets this category as its entire gros exposure to gross households (not limited 
to the exposure of the subsidiary bank s operating in the EU).

- What this section is: Part of the consolidated Management Report in the Integrated Annual Report 2024 presenting Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – turnover-based data under the EU Taxonomy, in HUF million, as of 31 December 2024, with 2023 comparatives (T-1).
- Scope of disclosure: Breaks down assets used for GAR calculation into GAR-covered assets (numerator and denominator), assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator, and assets not covered by GAR (e.g., central governments, central banks, trading book).
- Taxonomy dimensions reported: For each portfolio slice, shows taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned amounts across the six environmental objectives:
  - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM)
  - Climate Change Adaptation (CCA)
  - Water and Marine Resources (WTR)
  - Circular Economy (CE)
  - Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC)
  - Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)
  Including tags for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Portfolio breakdown: Detailed by instrument and counterparty type:
  - Loans and advances, debt securities, equity instruments (non-HfT, i.e., not held for trading).
  - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings).
  - Non-financial undertakings.
  - Households, with “of which” details for:
    - Loans collateralised by residential property.
    - Building renovation loans.
    - Motor vehicle loans.
  - Collateral obtained (residential and commercial real estate).
- GAR coverage and totals (2024):
  - Total assets: 44,852,131.
  - Total GAR assets (denominator): 29,047,630.
  - Assets not covered for GAR: 15,804,501 (notably central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book).
  - Across all six objectives for GAR-covered assets, taxonomy-eligible amount: 3,975,280; taxonomy-aligned amount: 30,365; enabling and transitional exposures are reported but remain small.
- Household portfolio (2024): Large taxonomy-eligible exposures reported, including:
  - Households total eligible: 3,822,141.
  - Of which mortgages: 3,422,059.
  - Building renovation loans: 127,014.
  - Motor vehicle loans: 273,068.
- Non-financial undertakings (2024): Material share of taxonomy-aligned exposures within CCM; total taxonomy-eligible across all objectives: 99,015; taxonomy-aligned: 28,139.
- Financial undertakings (2024): Credit institutions taxonomy-eligible across all objectives: 50,287.
- Assets excluded from numerator but in denominator (2024): 12,303,916, including SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD disclosure, non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, cash and cash-like items, and other assets (e.g., goodwill, commodities).
- Off-balance sheet (2024) for undertakings subject to NFRD:
  - Financial guarantees disclosed (no taxonomy amounts).
  - Assets under management: 4,346,946; taxonomy-eligible: 95,855; taxonomy-aligned: 15,963; with “of which” breakdown for debt and equity holdings.
- Comparative view (2023, T-1):
  - GAR-covered assets: 13,420,637; taxonomy-eligible: 3,018,478; taxonomy-aligned: 12,435.
  - Households eligible: 2,993,002 (mortgages 2,694,148; building renovation 127,416; motor vehicles 171,438).
  - Non-financial undertakings eligible: 21,188; aligned: 12,435.
- Overall purpose: To provide regulatory EU Taxonomy-aligned transparency on the bank’s GAR composition, eligibility and alignment by objective, activity type (use-of-proceeds, transitional, enabling), counterparty class, and instrument, including on- and off-balance sheet exposures, and to show year-on-year movement.

summary:
- Purpose and scope: Extract from the consolidated Management Report presenting EU Taxonomy and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures in HUF million for the banking group.
- Reference dates and views:
  - Turnover-based GAR (T-1) as of 31 Dec 2023.
  - Extended six-objective Taxonomy overview (adding Circular Economy, Pollution, Biodiversity) as of 31 Dec 2024, showing totals across objectives.
  - Capex-based GAR as of 31 Dec 2024.
- Coverage and breakdown:
  - Assets included in GAR numerator/denominator: loans and advances, debt securities (incl. use-of-proceeds), and equity not held for trading.
  - Counterparty types: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation, motor vehicle loans), and collateral obtained.
  - Off-balance sheet items: financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM), with split by debt and equity.
  - Tags disclosed per objective: Taxonomy-eligible vs. Taxonomy-aligned; and of which use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- Key totals and scope exclusions:
  - Total assets: HUF 39,609,144 million.
  - GAR-covered assets: HUF 25,679,052 million.
  - Assets excluded from the numerator but in denominator: HUF 11,562,435 million (incl. SMEs/NFCs not under NFRD, non‑EU counterparties, derivatives, on‑demand interbank, cash, other assets).
  - Assets not covered for GAR: HUF 13,930,092 million (central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, trading book).
- 2023 turnover-based highlights:
  - Taxonomy-eligible exposure concentrated in households for Climate Change Mitigation (CCM): HUF 2,993,002 million (incl. HUF 2,694,148 million mortgages; HUF 127,416 million building renovation loans).
  - Non-financial corporates: CCM eligible HUF 21,188 million, with CCM aligned HUF 12,435 million; small Water (WTR) eligibility/enabling (c. HUF 974–1,007 million).
  - Overall alignment remains limited relative to eligibility in 2023.
  - Off-balance sheet AUM: CCM eligible HUF 144,741 million, aligned c. HUF 10,195 million; with debt and equity instrument splits disclosed; footnote indicates restatement.
- 2024 six-objective total (consolidated view across CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO):
  - GAR-covered assets: total Taxonomy-eligible HUF 3,018,493 million; aligned HUF 12,435 million (largely in non-financial corporates).
  - AUM: eligible HUF 146,307 million; aligned HUF 11,371 million (with instrument-level splits).
  - Financial guarantees show no Taxonomy eligibility/alignment.
- 2024 capex-based highlights:
  - Total GAR assets assessed: HUF 16,727,599 million.
  - CCM eligibility HUF 4,002,781 million; CCA HUF 80,382 million; WTR HUF 767 million.
  - Alignment evident in credit institutions and non-financial corporates (e.g., credit institutions CCM aligned c. HUF 2,979 million; non-financial corporates CCM aligned c. HUF 77,275 million, with reported transitional/enabling/use-of-proceeds components).
  - Households drive large CCM eligibility (HUF 3,822,141 million), dominated by mortgages (HUF 3,422,059 million) and renovation loans (HUF 127,014 million); alignment for households not reported.
- Overall message: The group provides granular EU Taxonomy/GAR disclosures by objective, counterparty, and instrument, evidencing substantial Taxonomy-eligible exposure (especially to households) but comparatively modest Taxonomy-aligned exposure, with clearer alignment in selected corporate and financial counterparties under the capex-based view.

title: Assets for the calculation of GAR – Capex based
heading: 1. Assets for the calculation of GAR – Capex based
start_phrase: HUF million Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
- What it is: Consolidated Management Report tables presenting the EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – Capex-based – for the Group, with figures in HUF million as at 31 December 2024, plus a comparative (T-1) snapshot for 31 December 2023.
- Scope and structure:
  - GAR “covered assets” shown for both numerator and denominator.
  - Assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator are detailed.
  - Assets not covered for GAR calculation (e.g., central governments, central banks, trading book) are listed.
  - Off-balance sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD disclosure obligations are included (financial guarantees; assets under management, with security type split).
  - Breakdowns by counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments), and by instrument (loans and advances, debt securities incl. use-of-proceeds bonds, equity instruments, collateral obtained).
- Environmental coverage:
  - Disclosures by EU Taxonomy environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each objective: taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned amounts, including sub-classifications for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- 2024 headline figures:
  - Total assets: 44,852,131.
  - Total GAR assets (denominator scope): 29,047,630.
  - Total taxonomy-eligible within GAR assets (across all six objectives): ~4,012,073.
  - Total taxonomy-aligned within GAR assets (across all six objectives): ~82,911, with small portions tagged as use-of-proceeds, transitional, or enabling.
- Key composition insights (2024):
  - Loans, advances, and non-trading securities form the core of GAR-covered assets (16,727,599).
  - Households represent a large share of taxonomy-eligible CCM exposures (3,822,141), mainly:
    - Residential mortgages (3,422,059).
    - Building renovation loans (127,014).
    - Motor vehicle loans (273,068).
    - No taxonomy-aligned amounts reported for households.
  - Non-financial undertakings:
    - Taxonomy-eligible total across objectives: ~136,207.
    - Taxonomy-aligned: ~79,783 (main aligned contributions reside here).
  - Financial undertakings:
    - Taxonomy-eligible: ~53,725.
    - Taxonomy-aligned: ~3,128.
  - Use-of-proceeds green bonds, transitional, and enabling categories are present but quantitatively small.
- Exclusions and other assets (2024):
  - Assets excluded from numerator but in denominator: 12,303,916, including:

summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures in the consolidated Management Report (Integrated Annual Report 2024), with Capex-based GAR figures as of 31 December 2023, presented in HUF million.
- Coverage and structure:
  - GAR-covered assets include loans and advances, debt securities and equity instruments not held for trading, split by counterparty (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households), plus collateral obtained.
  - Breakout by environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity (BIO), with flags for “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” activities (mostly zero).
- Key totals:
  - Total assets: 39,609,144.
  - Total GAR assets (denominator for GAR): 25,679,052.
  - Taxonomy-eligible within GAR assets: 3,038,192.
  - Taxonomy-aligned within GAR assets: 23,138.
- Composition of taxonomy-relevant exposures:
  - Households: 11,231,366 total; 2,993,002 taxonomy-eligible (incl. 2,694,148 residential mortgages, 127,416 building renovation loans, 171,438 motor vehicle loans); no aligned amounts disclosed for households.
  - Non-financial undertakings: 176,625 total; 41,833 eligible and 23,138 aligned (loans: 21,221 eligible/13,844 aligned; debt securities: 20,612 eligible/9,293 aligned).
  - Financial undertakings: 2,012,646 total; 3,358 eligible; no aligned amounts.
- Assets excluded from the numerator but included in the denominator: 11,562,435, comprising SMEs and other NFCs not subject to NFRD (6,860,587), non‑EU counterparties not subject to NFRD (2,524,756), derivatives (41,967), on‑demand interbank loans (574,648), cash and cash-related (605,799), and other assets (954,677).
- Assets not covered for GAR calculation: 13,930,092, including central governments and supranational issuers (6,307,758), central banks’ exposure (7,401,137), and trading book (221,197).
- Off-balance sheet:
  - Financial guarantees: 173,787.
  - Assets under management (AUM): 3,177,939; taxonomy-eligible 346,148 and aligned 21,012 across the six objectives (with debt securities 3,653 eligible/aligned and equity instruments 17,359 eligible/aligned); figures noted as restated. Earlier breakdowns also provided for CCM/CCA/WTR components.
- Sectoral (turnover-based) GAR information:
  - NACE 4‑digit breakdown for CCM/CCA/WTR showing [gross] carrying amounts and “of which environmentally sustainable” for non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD and for SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - Sectors covered include electricity and gas activities (3511–3514, 3522–3523), waste (3811), fuel retail (4730), real estate (6820, 6831), transport/logistics (4931, 4950), chemicals (2016, 2059), metals (2442–2443), telecom (6110–6120), and others, with selected lines showing sustainable portions.

summary:
- The excerpt is from the Management Report (Consolidated) of the 2024 Integrated Annual Report and presents Green Asset Ratio (GAR) sector information.
- It provides a granular, NACE 4-digit breakdown of exposures and taxonomy alignment, expressed in HUF million, distinguishing:
  - By environmental objective: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - By counterparty type: Non-financial corporates subject to NFRD and SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - By metric: gross carrying amount and “of which environmentally sustainable.”
- Turnover-based GAR table (pp. 201–202) lists 50 NACE codes with objective-by-objective amounts and a total taxonomy-aligned column per code.
- Capex-based GAR table (p. 203) similarly breaks down, by NACE code and counterparty type, the gross and environmentally sustainable portions for CCM, CCA, and WTR (with CE/PPC/BIO likely continued on following pages).
- The data show varying levels of taxonomy alignment across sectors, with some codes reporting zero alignment and others reporting partial to high alignment.
- Notable examples with significant environmentally sustainable amounts include codes such as 6420, 7010, 3511, 3512, 3513, 4931, 1062, 2059, and 2442; some lines show near/full alignment in specific objectives (e.g., 4730, 2442, 3513 in parts of the tables).
- Overall, the section evidences the institution’s EU Taxonomy disclosure by mapping turnover and capex to environmental objectives across sectors, highlighting the share of environmentally sustainable activities within its non-financial corporate portfolios.

- Overall purpose: to disclose sectoral and product/counterparty‑level distribution of green assets, in HUF, under EU Taxonomy/NFRD, using both capex‑based and turnover‑based GAR views.

summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPI Stock disclosures as of 31 December 2024, shown on a turnover-based and a capex-based basis.
- Covers all six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), and Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
- Breaks down GAR by:
  - Taxonomy-eligible vs. Taxonomy-aligned shares.
  - “Of which” categories: use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Asset classes and counterparties: loans and advances, debt securities (incl. UoP), equity instruments not held for trading; financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments, and repossessed collateral.
- Key outcomes (turnover-based):
  - Total GAR-eligible assets around 13.7% of covered assets; Taxonomy-aligned share is very low (about 0.1%), almost entirely under CCM; alignment for other objectives is near zero.
  - GAR coverage equals 64.76% of total assets (proportion of total assets covered by the GAR denominator).
  - Eligibility largely driven by exposures to non-financial undertakings; financial undertakings contribute marginally; household exposures are substantial in size but currently show 0% eligibility/alignment under the taxonomy scopes applied.
- Key outcomes (capex-based):
  - Total GAR-eligible assets around 13.8%; Taxonomy-aligned share is modestly higher than in the turnover-based view (around 0.3%), again primarily under CCM; other objectives remain near zero.
  - Within non-financial undertakings, capex-based alignment is higher for certain instruments (e.g., debt securities), while use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling classifications remain negligible overall.
- Overall message: the bank’s taxonomy-eligible exposure is small relative to total covered assets, and taxonomy-aligned exposure is currently minimal, with non-financial corporate lending/securities providing the main source of eligibility.

title: GAR KPI Stock – Capex based
heading: 3. GAR KPI Stock – Capex based
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
- Presents the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs under the EU Taxonomy for the consolidated group, with detailed “stock” disclosures:
  - Capex‑based GAR as of 31 December 2024
  - Turnover‑based GAR (T‑1) as of 31 December 2023
- Breaks down GAR by the six environmental objectives:
  - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO)
- Reports, for each objective, the share of exposures that are:
  - Taxonomy‑eligible vs. Taxonomy‑aligned
  - Of which “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” activities
- Provides a granular split by counterparty and instrument:
  - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings)
  - Non‑financial undertakings
  - Households (including sub‑categories such as residential mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
  - Local governments and collateral obtained
  - Instrument types: loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds bonds), equity instruments, with exclusions for HfT items
- Key headline figures shown:
  - 2024 Capex‑based “Total GAR assets”: 13.8% taxonomy‑eligible and 0.3% taxonomy‑aligned; of which 0.2% transitional; GAR denominator covers 64.76% of total assets
  - 2023 Turnover‑based “Total GAR assets”: 10.4% taxonomy‑eligible with negligible/zero alignment reported
- Highlights sectoral contributions:
  - Non‑financial undertakings account for most taxonomy‑eligible/aligned exposures
  - Households and local government exposures are largely non‑eligible, though included in the GAR denominator
- Includes proportional shares of total assets covered for each category, enabling readers to see how much of the balance sheet is in scope for GAR calculations

title: GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based (T-1)
heading: 3. GAR KPI Stock – Turnover based (T-1)
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2023
summary:
- Context: Consolidated Management Report within the Integrated Annual Report 2024 disclosing EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) KPIs as of 31 December 2023. Two GAR “stock” views are shown: Turnover-based (T-1) and Capex-based (T-1).
- Scope and structure: Detailed breakdowns of covered assets in both numerator and denominator by counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments), asset class (loans and advances, debt securities including use-of-proceeds, equity instruments), and by environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and marine resources, Circular Economy, Pollution, Biodiversity). “Use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” subcategories are also reported. A “Proportion of total assets covered” column quantifies coverage.
- Key results (Turnover-based):
  - Total GAR assets show eligibility only for Climate Change Mitigation (10.4% of covered assets); other environmental objectives report 0% eligibility. Taxonomy-aligned shares are effectively negligible (≈0.1% in one category; otherwise 0.0%).
  - Non-financial undertakings provide the bulk of eligibility (e.g., 12.0% overall; loans 16.6%, debt securities 9.6%), with small adaptation/water eligibility traces in debt securities (≈0.8–0.9%) and non-financial undertakings (≈0.6%), but alignment remains near zero.
  - Financial undertakings, credit institutions, and sub-sectors (investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings) show near-zero eligibility/alignment.
  - Households are sizeable in covered assets (26.7% overall; with sub-portfolios: 59.5% residential mortgages, 99.8% building renovation loans, 38.4% motor vehicle loans) but show 0% taxonomy eligibility/alignment.
  - Proportion of total assets covered: overall ≈64.83%; notable items include 29.92% for loans/debt/equity not HfT-eligible for GAR, 25.04% households, 10.09% mortgages, 0.28% building renovation loans, 1.00% motor vehicle loans.
  - “Use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” classifications are reported at 0% across categories.
- Key results (Capex-based):
  - Similar overall pattern with Climate Change Mitigation eligibility at 10.3% of covered assets; no eligibility reported for other objectives; alignment remains negligible.
  - Higher eligibility within non-financial undertakings compared to the turnover view (23.7% overall; loans 34.9%; debt securities 17.8%); alignment still ≈0%.
  - Financial undertakings and households mirror the turnover-based outcome (near-zero eligibility/alignment for financials; households large but non-contributing to taxonomy eligibility).
- Other notes: Local government financing and repossessed collateral are listed with 0% eligibility/alignment. Overall, eligibility is concentrated in climate change mitigation exposures to non-financial corporates, with very limited taxonomy-aligned assets reported.

title: GAR KPI Stock – Capex based (T-1)
heading: 3. GAR KPI Stock – Capex based (T-1)
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2023
summary:
- Presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures in the Management Report (Consolidated) of the Integrated Annual Report 2024, covering both:
  - GAR KPI Stock – Capex-based (T-1), reference date 31 Dec 2023
  - GAR KPI Flow – Turnover-based, reference date 31 Dec 2024
- Scope and structure:
  - Metrics reported by environmental objective: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution (PPC), and Biodiversity (BIO)
  - Distinguishes Taxonomy-eligible vs Taxonomy-aligned exposures, and “of which” sub-categories: use-of-proceeds instruments, transitional activities, enabling activities
  - Broken down by counterparty/asset class: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non-financial undertakings, households (mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments, and collateral obtained
  - Coverage indicator: proportion of total assets included in the GAR denominator
- Key stock (Capex-based, 2023) takeaways:
  - Overall coverage: 64.83% of total assets are in the GAR scope
  - Total GAR assets show 10.3% Taxonomy-eligible for CCM; other objectives (CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO) report 0% at total level; Taxonomy-aligned totals are largely 0%
  - Non-financial undertakings drive most eligibility/alignment within CCM; financial undertakings and local governments show negligible figures
  - Households portfolio is materially represented in scope; sub-categories indicate high taxonomy relevance of building renovation loans (99.8%) and significant inclusion of mortgages; however, aligned amounts reported for households are 0%
  - Collateral obtained (residential/commercial) is negligible in scope
- Key flow (Turnover-based, 2024) takeaways:
  - Total GAR assets indicate 13.0% CCM Taxonomy-eligible and 0.1% aligned; CCA and WTR show minimal to zero values; CE/PPC/BIO not reported with eligible/aligned values
  - Non-financial undertakings contribute the majority of CCM eligibility and the limited alignment observed; loans and advances dominate, with some exposure via debt securities (including use-of-proceeds instruments)
  - Households again feature prominently for CCM eligibility (e.g., high shares for mortgages and building renovation loans such as 65.1% and 99.5% taxonomy relevance respectively), but no aligned amounts are reported
  - Financial undertakings and local governments remain near zero across objectives
- Overall message:
  - GAR exposures are concentrated in Climate Change Mitigation, with minimal or no reported eligibility/alignment for other environmental objectives
  - Alignment levels are low relative to eligibility, and much of the portfolio—especially households—appears eligible but not yet reported as aligned
  - The report provides granular breakdowns by asset class and counterparty, including identification of use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities, most of which are minimal or zero in the period reported.

- Scope: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures presented on:
  - Turnover-based data (pages 213–214)
  - Capex-based data (page 215)
- Environmental objectives covered: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and marine resources (WTR), Circular economy (CE), Pollution prevention and control (PPC), Biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
- Metrics shown for each objective and asset class:
  - Taxonomy-eligible share and Taxonomy-aligned share
  - Of which: use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR denominator
- Breakdown by counterparty and instrument:
  - Financial undertakings (incl. credit institutions, other financial corporations, investment firms, management companies, insurance undertakings)
  - Non-financial undertakings (loans and advances; debt securities incl. use-of-proceeds; equity instruments)
  - Households (of which: loans collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
  - Local governments (housing financing; other) and collateral obtained (immovable properties)
- Key highlights (Turnover-based):
  - Total GAR assets (all objectives combined): 13.04% taxonomy-eligible; 0.13% taxonomy-aligned; GAR coverage: 58.52% of total assets
  - Non-financial undertakings are the main source of eligible/aligned exposure; financial undertakings mostly negligible
  - Household exposures are large in coverage (notably mortgages) but show minimal taxonomy eligibility/alignment in the presented figures; building renovation and motor vehicle loan sub-lines are reported
  - Use-of-proceeds, transitional and enabling contributions are minimal across categories
- Key highlights (Capex-based; objectives shown: CCM/CCA/WTR):
  - Total GAR assets: CCM 13.3% taxonomy-eligible; 0.4% taxonomy-aligned; negligible values reported for CCA and WTR at total level
  - Non-financial undertakings (especially debt securities including use-of-proceeds) drive higher eligibility/alignment under the capex view
- Overall: Detailed quantitative templates map the bank’s covered assets to EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment, by counterparty and instrument, distinguishing activity types and indicating the share of total assets included in the GAR calculation.

heading: 4. GAR KPI Flow – Capex based
start_phrase: % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator) Disclosure reference date 31 December 2024
summary:
This excerpt presents the bank’s EU Taxonomy disclosures as of 31 December 2024, focusing on:
- GAR KPI Flow – Capex based: A detailed table of Green Asset Ratio metrics for on-balance sheet assets included in both numerator and denominator. It breaks down exposures by environmental objectives (Climate Change Mitigation, Climate Change Adaptation, Water and Marine Resources, Circular Economy, Pollution Prevention and Control, Biodiversity and Ecosystems), distinguishing taxonomy-eligible vs. taxonomy-aligned shares and further classifying aligned exposures into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling. The scope covers loans and advances, debt securities and equity not held for trading, split across financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations including investment firms, management companies, insurance), non-financial undertakings, households (residential mortgages, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans), local governments, and collateral obtained. The table also shows the proportion of total assets covered. Headline signals include very limited taxonomy alignment overall, with concentrations in climate change mitigation exposures to non-financial undertakings and eligibility indications in household portfolios; many other segments and objectives register near-zero values. The summary row indicates total CCM eligibility of 13.3% and 0.4% aligned within GAR-covered assets, with total assets coverage of 58.52%.
- KPI off-balance sheet exposures (Stock) – Turnover based: Taxonomy KPIs for financial guarantees and assets under management. Financial guarantees show no eligible or aligned exposures. Assets under management show small taxonomy-eligible and aligned shares, primarily linked to climate change mitigation, with a total eligible share of 2.2% and 0.4% aligned (including 0.3% enabling).
