title: Green lending target
heading: Green lending target
start_phrase: As in its ESG strategy declared in 2021, OTP Group's unchanged goal is to play a regional leading role in financing a fair and gradual transition to a low -carbon economy and to build a sustainable future with responsible solutions.81
summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s green lending ambitions and climate-related operational targets within the 2024 Integrated Annual Report.
- Green lending target: Build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025, aiming to lead regionally in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy.
- Scope of green exposures: Includes corporate green loans and bonds, plus retail green loans per OTP Group’s internal definition.
- Country coverage: Green lending pursued in all countries except Russia (consumer lending dominates) and Ukraine (war prevents standards‑compliant green lending).
- Nature of target: Not science‑based; aligned with business objective to finance transition and drive revenue growth; developed with input from relevant OTP departments.
- Progress: Group green exposure has been measured since 2022 and shows steady growth through 2024, with a plan to reach HUF 1,500 billion in 2025 (2024 around HUF 1,027 billion).
- Operational climate targets: No group‑level mitigation target yet; some subsidiaries have partial Scope 1–2 targets. A Paris‑aligned, group‑level target is planned for 2026. Emissions are monitored, but reduction effectiveness is not yet measured.
- OTP Bank (parent) target: Carbon‑neutral operations by 2030 for Scope 1–2 (absolute net‑zero, no base year specified), not science‑based; departments involved in setting the goal.
- 2024 emissions: OTP Bank market‑based Scope 1–2 emissions were 6,644 tCO2e; electricity largely from green energy; ~75% of emissions from natural gas and vehicle fuel. A property and fleet emissions‑intensity reduction plan is in preparation, to be finalized in 2025.
- Reporting notes: Green financing spans all ESRS climate subtopics; comparability with prior years is limited due to ESRS methodology changes.
text:
Green lending target   
As in its ESG strategy declared in 2021, OTP Group's unchanged goal is to play a regional leading role in 
financing a fair and gradual transition to a low -carbon economy and to build a sustainable future with 
responsible solutions.81  
The Banking Group plans to build a green loan portfolio worth HUF 1,500 billion by 2025 .  
Green lending is a goal in all countries except Russia and Ukraine. In Russia consumer lending is predominant, 
so green lending is not a goal. In Ukraine, due to the war, there is no green lending that meets the standards, 
and its development is not a goal until the conflict is resolved.  
  
Green exposures refer to corporate green loan and bond exposures, as well as retail green loan exposures, 
according to OTP Group's own definition (see. @green portfolio ).  
The goal for the green portfolio is not based on scientific evidence; it aligns with OTP Group's objective to 
finance the transition to a low -carbon economy. Achieving this goal will result in revenue growth for the 
corporate group. The relevant department s of OTP Group participated in setting this goal.

title: Additional targets
heading: Additional targets
start_phrase: We do not publish a group -level goal for operational activities related to climate change mitigation.
summary:
- OTP Group’s 2021 ESG strategy targets a regional leadership role in financing a fair, gradual transition to a low‑carbon economy.
- Green lending target: build a HUF 1,500 billion green loan portfolio by 2025 at group level. Green lending applies in all countries except Russia (consumer lending predominant) and Ukraine (war; no standard‑compliant green lending until conflict ends).
- Definition and governance: “Green exposures” include corporate green loans/bonds and retail green loans per OTP’s own taxonomy. The goal is not science‑based but aligned with transition financing and expected to drive revenue growth; relevant internal departments set the target. Green exposures have been measured since 2022.
- Progress toward target (end‑year group portfolio): 2022 HUF 267 bn; 2023 HUF 656 bn; 2024 HUF 1,027 bn; 2025 plan HUF 1,500 bn.
- Operational climate targets: no group‑level mitigation target yet; some subsidiaries have partial Scope 1–2 goals. A Paris‑aligned group target is planned for 2026. Emissions are monitored, but effectiveness of reduction measures is not comprehensively measured.
- OTP Bank (Hungary) operational goal: carbon‑neutral Scope 1–2 operations by 2030 (absolute net‑zero, no base year; not science‑based). 2024 market‑based Scope 1–2 emissions: 6,644 tCO2e. Electricity largely from green sources; ~75% of emissions from natural gas and vehicle fuels. A plan to cut property and fleet emissions intensity is being prepared for completion in 2025.
- Subsidiary actions: several foreign subsidiaries commit to reducing operational emissions, chiefly via green electricity procurement; monitoring occurs locally, with no group aggregation of effectiveness.
- Water, biodiversity, ecosystems: no group targets yet; only limited water‑related measures exist; effectiveness not monitored. Further impact assessment is needed before defining measures.
- Actions and resources (ESRS references): two main measure packages—(1) portfolio‑specific measures tied to climate target setting (ESRS E1‑4) and (2) green lending measures; OTP Fund Management contributes via funds with environmental objectives. Operational GHG reduction measures are less material and reported in aggregate.
- Scope 1–2 reduction measures underway/planned: green electricity purchasing (Hungary, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia in 2024; continuation in 2025), lighting/boiler replacements, HVAC optimization, insulation, solar panels. Serbia and Albania moved to more energy‑efficient HQs; Albania HQ is LEED Gold. Effectiveness tracked at subsidiary level; not consolidated.
- GHG emissions reporting: ESRS E1‑6 table (gross Scope 1, 2, 3) referenced; comparability with earlier years limited due to ESRS methodology changes.
text:
Additional targets  
We do not publish a group -level goal for operational activities related to climate change mitigation. Partial 
targets for Scope 1 -2 emissions currently exist at the subsidiary level for some subsidiaries. A group -level 
target, consistent with the Paris Agr eement and based on the same reference, is planned for 2026, with further 
details to be developed in the next period. Emissions are continuously monitored, but the effectiveness of 
measures to reduce emissions is not currently measured.  
OTP Bank's goal set in its 2021 ESG strategy is to achieve carbon -neutral operations by 2030. This absolute 
target covers Scope 1 -2 emissions, with a recorded net -zero emission of 0 tCO 2e, without specifying a base 
year. Net -zero emissions involve reducing greenhouse gas emissions as much as possible and neutralizing 
unavoidable emissions through carbon removal. The goal is not based on scientific evidence; the relevant 
departments of OTP  Bank participated in its development. OTP Bank's market -based Scope 1 -2 emissions 
were 6,644 tCO 2e in 202482. OTP Bank primarily uses green energy for electricity, with about three -quarters 
of emissions coming from natural gas use and vehicle fuel consumption. The preparation of a plan to reduce 
emissions intensity related to properties and the fleet has begun, with an ESG Committee resolution to 
complete it in 2025.  
 
81 Green financing is an objective in all three climate change -related subtopics named in the ESRS, and OTP Group does not treat these topics separately. 
We have not identified a base year for the objective; we have been measuring green exposures in the portf olio since 2022 .

text:
Actions and resources  
ESRS E1 -3, E3 -2, E4 -3 
OTP Group has defined two main packages of measures regarding climate change: firstly, the portfolio -specific 
measures defined within the climate target setting  detailed in the @E1 -4 disclosure requirement, and 
secondly, the green lending  measures83 presented in chapter @2.1. 2 and @Credit Rating . The measures of 
OTP Fund Management are represented by the funds with environmental objectives presented in chapter 
@2.1. 1. Measures to reduce GHG emissions from operations are of lesser significance and are presented in 
aggregate.  
Measures to Reduce Scope 1 -2 Emissions  
Primarily, the larger banks in the Banking Group are implementing or planning to implement measures to 
reduce carbon dioxide emissions. Among the planned measures, the procurement of green electricity has the 
greatest impact; in 2024 OTP Bank, OTP Bank Slo venia, OTP Bank Croatia, and OTP Bank Serbia mainly 
covered their consumption with green electricity. These practices are planned to continue in 2025. Additionally, 
planned measures include lighting replacement, boiler replacement, optimization of heating and cooling, 
insulation, and solar panel installation. OTP Bank Serbia and OTP Bank Albania have moved to more energy -
efficient central buildings, with the Albanian bank's headquarters being LEED Gold certified. The effectiveness 
of the implemented measure s is monitored at the subsidiary level using various methods, and the results are 
not aggregated.   
OTP Group has not yet defined measures related to biodiversity and ecosystems. A more detailed assessment 
of the impacts is necessary before developing appropriate measures.

heading: Scope 3 / Category 15 emissions in 2023
start_phrase: The below table provides an overview on OTP Group’s financed emissions (Scope 3 / Category 15) in 2023 by PCAF asset classes and by the type of emission scope of the clients.
summary:
- Context: Consolidated Management Report section of OTP Group’s Integrated Annual Report 2024, focusing on group-wide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and financed (Scope 3/Category 15) emissions, methods, and targets.

- System boundaries and notes:
  - “Base year 2023” reflects OTP Group as of 31 Dec 2023; “Comparative 2023” reflects the 2024 group composition; methodologies are otherwise unchanged.
  - Scope 3 totals exclude emissions tied to assets managed by OTP’s fund manager subsidiaries (not owned/ consolidated).
  - 2023 Scope 3 totals exclude OTP Bank Romania group.
  - Biogenic emissions in 2024: 734 tCO2e.

- Operational (Scopes 1–2) emissions, 2024:
  - Scope 1 gross emissions: 118,470 tCO2e; 0% under regulated ETS.
  - Scope 2 gross emissions: 58,076 tCO2e (location-based); 48,834 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Electricity sourcing: 36.49% of electricity backed by guarantees of origin/RECs; 31.23% of Scope 2-related energy consumption certified; no certified district heating.

- Total GHG emissions, 2024:
  - 25,012,535 tCO2e (identical for location- and market-based totals due to Scope 3 dominance).

- GHG intensity based on revenue, 2024:
  - 5.85 tCO2e per million HUF of net revenue (both location- and market-based).

- Significant Scope 3 (Category 15 – Investments):
  - Totals:
    - 2023: 25,007,832 tCO2e (base and comparative, with scope caveats above).
    - 2024: 24,835,989 tCO2e (–1% vs 2023).
    - Target: 16,855,279 tCO2e by 2030, implying a –5.5% annual reduction from the 2023 base.
  - OTP’s preferred financed emissions indicator: sum of financed Scope 1–2 (excluding sovereigns) at 9.2 MtCO2e in 2023, citing high uncertainty in Scope 3 and sovereign estimates.
  - Portfolio drivers (2023):
    - Business loans contribute ~73% of financed Scope 1–2; vehicle financing ~20%; real estate-related portfolios are a small share.
  - Financed emissions intensity (emissions/outstanding volume, 2023):
    - Financed Scope 1–2 intensity excluding sovereigns: 0.57 g CO2e/HUF.
    - Most GHG-intensive segments: corporate/business loans and vehicle financing.
  - PCAF reporting (2023):
    - Asset-class breakdowns provided with exposures, financed Scope 1/2/3, and average data quality scores (overall 3.5 incl. sovereigns; 4.3 excluding).
    - Total across all PCAF classes (incl. sovereigns): 25,007,832 tCO2e; sovereign debt: 4,608,884 tCO2e.
  - 2024 financed emissions: preliminary estimates prepared using the same methodology but on less complete data due to unavailability of 2024 borrower financials before reporting cut-offs.

- Internal allocation of operational emissions, 2024:
  - Consolidated financial reporting group vs operational management:
    - Scope 1: 114,940 tCO2e vs 3,530 tCO2e.
    - Scope 2 (location-based): 53,668 tCO2e vs 4,409 tCO2e.
    - Scope 2 (market-based): 41,561 tCO2e vs 7,273 tCO2e.

title: Financed GHG emissions (Scope 3 / Category 15) of OTP Group in 2024
heading: Financed GHG emissions (Scope 3 / Category 15) of OTP Group in 2024
start_phrase: OTP Group prepared a preliminary estimation for its financed emissions for 2024.
summary:
- Focus: OTP Group’s financed greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) reported under the PCAF standard, with detailed breakdowns by asset class for 2023 (excluding OBR Group) and preliminary estimates for 2024, plus financed-emission intensities and data quality notes.
- Asset classes covered: listed equity and corporate bonds; business loans, unlisted equity and project loans; commercial real estate financing; mortgages; vehicle loans; and sovereign debt (tracked separately and excluded from the main climate target).
- 2023 highlights:
  - Total exposure: ~HUF 22.1 trillion; average PCAF data quality score: 3.5.
  - Key metric for targets: financed Scope 1–2 intensity excluding sovereigns = 0.57 g CO2e/HUF.
  - Most GHG-intensive segments: corporate/business lending and vehicle financing.
  - Emission intensities by asset class show highest values in vehicle loans and business lending; mortgages and commercial real estate are much lower. Some scope items are marked n.a. where not applicable.
- 2024 preliminary estimates:
  - Total exposure: ~HUF 26.7 trillion; average PCAF data quality score: 3.3.
  - Total financed emissions across scopes reported by asset class; financed Scope 1–2 intensity excluding sovereigns = 0.47 g CO2e/HUF, a 19% decrease vs 2023.
  - Drivers of the decline: HUF depreciation vs EUR; repayment by major polluters; reduced attribution factors as some borrowers’ balance sheets grew while OTP loans stayed flat; lower share of heavy machinery in vehicle financing; and changes in data quality. Most drivers are outside OTP’s control.
  - Caution: the decline should not be seen as a trend; OTP flags limitations and low robustness in PCAF methodology, noting potential for reversal next year.
  - Asset-class intensities remain highest in vehicle loans, then business loans and listed equity/corporate bonds; mortgages and commercial real estate stay low; sovereign intensity drops from 0.76 to 0.67 g CO2e/HUF.
- Data limitations: 2024 estimates are based on less complete borrower data due to reporting lags (e.g., 2024 financials available only by May 2025), affecting estimation certainty.
- Managed assets: Group asset/fund managers’ financed emissions estimated at ~5.8 Mt CO2e in 2024 (coverage-adjusted), calculated by MSCI (real estate funds internally). These are not included in OTP Group’s consolidated financed emissions because the assets are not owned or consolidated.
text:
OTP Group prepared a preliminary estimation for its financed emissions for 2024. These estimations were 
based on the same approach as in the estimates for 2023, however on less complete data. The underlying 
reason for the latter is that much essential data84 to quantify the financed emissions of OTP Group was not 
available before the cut -off date of the recent Integrated Report.  
 
84 For example: financial figures (such as total assets and revenues) of corporate borrowers for the business year of 2024, beca use these will have to 
be published only by May 2025 in many countries, whereas calculations of financed GHG emissions of OTP Grou p had to be submitted to the auditor by 
the beginning of February 2024.

The financed GHG intensity of OTP Group (financed emissions / financed volume) in 2024, according to the 
most relevant indicator with the smallest estimation uncertainty, was 0.47 g CO 2eq / HUF, which is 19% lower 
than in 2023. This significant decrease can be explained by several factors: the weakening of the HUF against 
the EUR in the meantime (excluding the exchange rate effect, the change in Group's financed GHG intensity 
would have been only -13%). Other reasons for the decrease include: some major polluters repaid their loans, 
other larger polluters significantly increased their balance sheets while the loans provided by the Banking 
Group remained unchanged (thus the "attribution factor" allocating the debtor's GHG emissions to Group 
decreased), and the financing ratio of heavy machinery, which is mor e GHG -intensive, decreased in the vehicle 
financing portfolio. In addition, changes in the quality of the data used also affected the results. Overall, it can 
be said that OTP Group had no influence on most of the factors causing the decrease in its financ ed carbon 
footprint and will not have any influence in the future. Therefore, it is important to emphasize that the 
decreasing trend observed between 2023 and 2024 cannot be projected into the future; on the contrary, this 
relatively significant change in the Group's financed GHG emissions highlights the shortcomings and low 
robustness of the carbon footprint calculation methodology defined by the PCAF standard, so a similar 
magnitude but opposite change cannot be ruled out in the next year.

summary:
- Presents OTP Group’s 2024 financed emissions (Scope 3/Category 15) by PCAF asset classes, including exposures, financed Scope 1/2/3, totals, and average data quality scores; sovereign debt is reported separately.
- Details portfolio emission intensities (g CO2e/HUF) by asset class and in total; overall financed GHG intensity was 0.47 g CO2e/HUF in 2024, 19% lower than 2023.
- Explains drivers of the intensity decrease: HUF/EUR FX effect, repayment by major emitters, changes in borrower balance sheets reducing attribution factors, lower share of heavy machinery in vehicle financing, and data quality changes; warns results are not predictive and highlights PCAF methodology limitations and potential volatility.
- Reports financed emissions of assets managed by OTP’s asset/fund managers at an estimated 5.8 MtCO2e (coverage-adjusted) for 2024; estimates by MSCI except real estate funds; these are not counted in OTP Group’s financed emissions because the assets are not owned/consolidated.
- Describes carbon credits and removals: OTP Bank retired 7,000 tCO2e VCS (Verra) credits from the St. Nikola Wind Farm (Bulgaria) to cover Scope 1–2; not a corresponding adjustment under Paris Agreement Article 6; net-zero Scope 1–2 by 2030 remains the goal. Plans to transition from offsets to ecosystem restoration certificates.
- Outlines a 400-hectare Budakeszi Vadaskert urban forest project with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt to support biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, employee engagement, ecotourism, and corporate image.
- Confirms no internal carbon pricing is applied.
- Notes transition plan and biodiversity considerations are disclosed under ESRS E4-1 with reference to ESRS 2 SBM-3.
- Defines green lending/green portfolio reporting: on-balance green exposures that pass internal green rating and meet criteria of OTP Group Green Loan Framework, OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework, and Hungarian National Bank programs (green housing, green corporate and municipal capital requirement discounts, NHP Green Home), which set baseline criteria.

OTP Group does not consider the funded issuance related to the assets managed by the fund and asset

title: GHG removals and carbon credits and Internal carbon pricing
heading: GHG removals and carbon credits and Internal carbon pricing
start_phrase: In 2024, within the corporate group, OTP Bank purchased carbon credits amounting to 7,000 tCO 2e.
summary:
- Reports financed GHG emissions for OTP Group’s fund and asset management activities in 2024, split by asset class with PCAF data quality scores:
  - Assets not in real estate funds: PCAF score 3.7; managed assets HUF 4,209 billion; financed emissions Scope 1–2: 1,616,427 tCO2e; Scope 3: 3,210,721 tCO2e; total: 4,827,148 tCO2e.
  - Assets in real estate funds: PCAF score 5.0; managed assets HUF 691 billion; financed emissions Scope 1–2: 4,055 tCO2e; Scope 3: 16,386 tCO2e; total: 20,441 tCO2e.
- Describes GHG removals and carbon credits (ESRS E1-7, E1-8): OTP Bank purchased and retired 7,000 tCO2e of Verra VCS credits covering Scope 1–2, sourced from the Sant Nikola Wind Farm in Bulgaria; notes the project is a mitigation project without Article 6 corresponding adjustments.
- Affirms carbon-neutral operations strategy and a net-zero Scope 1–2 target by 2030 through energy efficiency and renewables; plans to shift from carbon credits to ecosystem restoration certificates for operational footprint compensation.
- Outlines a biodiversity and ecosystem initiative with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400-hectare Budakeszi Vadaskert urban forest, prioritizing conservation and public welfare, supporting research and collaboration on biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, ecosystem services, employee awareness, and brand positioning.
- States no internal carbon pricing is applied.
- Notes transition plan and biodiversity considerations are disclosed under ESRS E4-1 via ESRS 2 SBM-3.
- Sets reporting policy for “chapter E” and defines green lending criteria for the voluntary Green Portfolio Report: green exposures are those with an internal green rating meeting technical screening under OTP Group Green Loan and Sustainable Finance Frameworks, Hungarian National Bank green housing/corporate/municipal capital requirement discount programs, and NHP Green Home; the Hungarian National Bank’s 2020–2021 programs form the baseline criteria.
text:
GHG removals and carbon credits and Internal carbon pricing  
ESRS E1 -7, E1 -8 
In 2024, within the corporate group, OTP Bank purchased carbon credits amounting to 7,000 tCO 2e. This 
amount covers OTP Bank's total Scope 1 -2 emissions. The carbon credits retired during the reporting period 
were verified according to the Verified Carbon Standard by Verra.  The Bank considers it essential that the 
project supported through the offsetting is implemented in the country where the Banking Group operates. 
Therefore, the only project supported by the purchase is the Sant Nikola Wind Farm near Kav arna, Bulgaria, 
which is the largest wind farm in the country. The project is a reduction project and does not qualify as a 
corresponding adjustment under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.85       
OTP Bank's goal of carbon -neutral operations includes the use of carbon credits as well. The use of carbon 
credits does not hinder the achievement of the net -zero target for Scope 1 -2 by 2030, considering that OTP 
Bank has begun developing emission reduction plans based on e nergy efficiency and renewable energy use. 
Additionally, as compensation for the Bank's operational carbon footprint, we plan to replace the carbon credits 
purchased based on our current practice with so -called ‘ecosystem restoration certificates’.  
In collaboration with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. as a partner, we aim to develop a 400 -hectare nature conservation 
area, the so -called Budakeszi Vadaskert, with a complex urban forest approach. This development somewhat 
places the economic aspects of the classic  triad of forest functions – economic, conservation, and public 
welfare – into the background in order to preserve and enhance the natural and ecological values of forests 
and promote ecotourism development that aligns with the natural values of forest are as.  The Bank has multiple 
goals in regard to this project: it offers a platform for professional collaborations and scientific work in 
biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, and ecosystem services.  On the other hand, it is 
suitable for promoting sustainability awareness among our employees by focusing on the non -financial aspects 
of forest area usage; furthermore, the project can also shape the Bank's image.  
The corporate group does not apply internal carbon pricing.

title: Green lending criteria and definitions used in the voluntary Green Portfolio Report
heading: Green lending criteria and definitions used in the voluntary Green Portfolio Report
start_phrase: Green exposure defined based on the bank's green definition: on -balance loans, advances, leasing, and bond exposures that have undergone an internal green rating process and meet the technical screening criteria of any of the following frameworks: OTP Group Green Loan Framework , OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework , the green housing, green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian National Bank, and the NHP Green Home.
summary:
- Reports financed GHG emissions for assets managed by OTP Group’s fund and asset management entities in 2024, split by asset class with PCAF data quality, managed assets, and coverage-adjusted emissions:
  - Assets not in real estate funds: PCAF score 3.7; HUF 4,209 billion managed; Scope 1–2: 1,616,427 tCO2e; Scope 3: 3,210,721 tCO2e; Total: 4,827,148 tCO2e.
  - Assets in real estate funds: PCAF score 5.0; HUF 691 billion managed; Scope 1–2: 4,055 tCO2e; Scope 3: 16,386 tCO2e; Total: 20,441 tCO2e.

- Describes GHG removals, carbon credits, and internal carbon pricing (ESRS E1-7, E1-8):
  - OTP Bank retired 7,000 tCO2e of Verra VCS credits in 2024, covering Scope 1–2, supporting the Sant Nikola Wind Farm in Bulgaria; a mitigation project without Article 6 corresponding adjustments.
  - Carbon-neutral operations strategy includes credits while pursuing energy efficiency and renewable energy to achieve Scope 1–2 net zero by 2030.
  - Plans to shift from carbon credits to ecosystem restoration certificates.
  - Partnership with Pilisi Parkerdő Zrt. to develop the 400-hectare Budakeszi Vadaskert urban forest for biodiversity, climate adaptation, carbon sequestration, ecosystem services, employee engagement, and reputation building.
  - No internal carbon pricing applied.

- Notes on transition plan and biodiversity integration (ESRS E4-1), disclosed under ESRS 2 SBM-3.

- Outlines reporting policy for Chapter E and green lending criteria:
  - Definition of green exposure for the voluntary Green Portfolio based on internal green rating and alignment with OTP Group Green Loan Framework, OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework, Hungarian National Bank (MNB) green capital requirement discount programs, and the NHP Green Home program.
  - National MNB programs (2020–2021) provide baseline criteria; EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment addressed in the OTP frameworks.
  - Green criteria for non-financial corporates anchored in OTP frameworks and MNB program; these underpin the voluntary green lending portfolio.
  - OTP Group Green Loan Framework updated with SPO and approved by MNB in July 2023; qualifying loans recognized as “Category B” under the MNB program; coverage spans large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
  - Retail green lending centered on MNB’s Green housing capital requirement discount and NHP Green Home, aligned with Hungarian/EU rules (e.g., 9/2023 Decree on building energy performance and NZEB).

- Clarifies differences between mandatory EU Taxonomy GAR KPIs and the voluntary green portfolio:
  - Voluntary GAR: centrally maintained, monthly monitoring, includes non-NFRD clients and non-EU exposures; expert-based criteria assessment.
  - Mandatory GAR: semi-annual, per EU 2021/2178; uses prescribed Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts, focusing on NFRD corporates with unknown use of proceeds and on exposures with known aligned use of proceeds.

- Details Scope 1–2 emissions boundaries and methodology:
  - 50.a: Emissions from assets within the IFRS-consolidated group (financial control), including IFRS 16 assets.
  - 50.b: Emissions from entities/arrangements under operational control outside full consolidation (associates, JVs, jointly controlled operations/assets).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; ETS-related Scope 1 not relevant.
  - Same calculation approach for 50.a and 50.b; estimates used where invoices are missing, with immaterial uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuel/energy, natural gas, and refrigerants from air conditioners/server coolers; CH4 and N2O from biogenic sources accounted separately; biofuel content uses defaults or actuals when available.
text:
Green lending criteria and definitions used in the voluntary Green Portfolio Report  
Green exposure defined based on the bank's green definition: on -balance loans, advances, leasing, and bond 
exposures that have undergone an internal green rating process and meet the technical screening criteria of 
any of the following frameworks: OTP Group Green Loan Framework , OTP Group Sustainable Finance 
Framework , the green housing, green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program of the 
Hungarian National Bank, and the NHP Green Home.   
As for all Hungarian banks, the main criteria that underpin the bank's green definitions are the Green housing 
capital requirement discount program 2020 -2021 and the Green corporate and municipal capital requirement 
discount program 2020 -2021 of the Hungar ian National Bank. These national programs define the baseline 
criteria for the green portfolios reported by the Bank.   
 
85 The project is 100% a mitigation project, implemented 100% in the E U, and certified 100% based on recognized quality standards.   
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  257 For information on the compliance with the EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment criteria of the bank's 
framework, please see  
@OTP Group Green Loan Framework   
@OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework  
Green criteria for non -financial corporations are set out in the following frameworks:  
• OTP Group Green Lending Framework  
• OTP Group Sustainable Finance Framework  
• Green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian National Bank   
These frameworks form the basis of OTP Bank's voluntary green lending portfolio.   
The update of the @OTP Group Green Loan Framework , also supported by an external expert opinion (SPO), 
was approved by the Hungarian National Bank in July 2023. This also ensures that loans that meet the 
conditions of the Bank's Framework are eligible for the Green corporate and municipal capital requirement 
discount program of the Hungarian National Bank as „Category B” transactions, which defines the scope of 
"eligible transactions under a Framework".  
The Green Loan Framework covers nonresidential customers, from large multinational corporations to micro -
enterprises, including municipalities and condominiums.

title: Retail green lending
heading: Retail green lending
start_phrase: In terms of residential green lending, the Green housing capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian National Bank and the NHP's Green Home program form the core of the lending.
summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy: references to eligibility and alignment through the OTP Group Green Loan and Sustainable Finance frameworks.
- Green lending foundations: OTP Group Green Lending Framework, Sustainable Finance Framework, and the Hungarian National Bank’s (HNB) green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program as the basis for the voluntary green lending portfolio.
- 2023 update: Green Loan Framework updated with a Second Party Opinion and approved by the HNB in July 2023; loans meeting the Framework qualify as “Category B” under the HNB discount program.
- Scope of Green Loan Framework: covers nonresidential customers from large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
- Retail green lending: anchored in HNB’s Green housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program, aligned with Hungarian and EU rules (e.g., Decree 9/2023 and NZEB requirements).
- Differences between voluntary green portfolio and mandatory EU Taxonomy metrics: the voluntary GAR portfolio is centrally maintained, monitored monthly, includes non-NFRD entities and non-EU exposures, with expert-based assessments; mandatory GAR KPIs are compiled semi-annually per EU 2021/2178 using Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts for NFRD corporates (unknown use of proceeds) and known aligned exposures.
- Scope 1–2 GHG emissions methodology and boundaries: 
  - 50.a financial control boundary for consolidated IFRS entities (including IFRS 16 assets).
  - 50.b operational control for non-consolidated entities (associates, JVs, unconsolidated subs, and joint arrangements).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; same calculation approach for 50.a and 50.b.
  - Estimates used when invoices are missing with immaterial uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuels/energy, natural gas, and HVAC/server cooling; CH4 and N2O from biogenic emissions reported separately; biofuel ratios use defaults unless specific data available.

Retail green lending  
In terms of residential green lending, the Green housing capital requirement discount program of the Hungarian

title: Main differences between the mandatory EU taxonomy indicators and the voluntary green portfolio:
heading: Main differences between the mandatory EU taxonomy indicators and the voluntary green portfolio:
start_phrase: The voluntary GAR portfolio is defined in a centrally maintained Group controlling database, monitored monthly, and extends to companies and households that are not subject to NFRD, as well as those outside the EU.
summary:
- Overview of OTP Group’s green finance approach, referencing core frameworks for EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment: OTP Group Green Loan Framework and Sustainable Finance Framework.
- Green criteria for non-financial corporates guided by OTP frameworks and the Hungarian National Bank’s (HNB) green corporate and municipal capital requirement discount program.
- Update to the OTP Group Green Loan Framework approved by the HNB in July 2023, supported by a Second Party Opinion, enabling “Category B” eligibility under the HNB discount program for loans meeting framework criteria.
- Scope of the Green Loan Framework covers nonresidential customers, from large corporates to micro-enterprises, municipalities, and condominiums.
- Retail green lending anchored in the HNB Green Housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program; alignment with Hungarian and EU rules (e.g., 9/2023 Decree on building energy performance and NZEB requirements).
- Distinction between voluntary green portfolio (GAR) and mandatory EU Taxonomy indicators: the voluntary GAR is centrally maintained, monitored monthly, includes EU and non-EU clients and households beyond NFRD scope, with expert-based eligibility assessment.
- Mandatory GAR KPIs are prepared semi-annually per EU 2021/2178, using Taxonomy KPIs and gross carrying amounts: includes NFRD corporate exposures with unknown use of proceeds and exposures with known, Taxonomy-aligned use of proceeds.
- Scope 1–2 GHG emissions boundaries: 
  - 50.a: assets within the IFRS-consolidated group under financial control (including IFRS 16).
  - 50.b: operationally controlled entities and arrangements outside 50.a (associates, JVs, unconsolidated subs, joint operations/assets).
- The Group is not subject to emissions trading schemes; thus ETS-related Scope 1 emissions are not applicable.

text:
Main differences between the mandatory EU taxonomy indicators and the voluntary green portfolio:  
The voluntary GAR portfolio is defined in a centrally maintained Group controlling database, monitored 
monthly, and extends to companies and households that are not subject to NFRD, as well as those outside 
the EU. Compliance with criteria is assessed by t he Bank's experts.  
In contrast, the mandatory GAR KPIs of the OTP Group are prepared semi -annually with the help of dedicated 
internal data requests, in accordance with the methodology prescribed by the regulation – EU 2021/2178, 
using only the Taxonomy KPIs and their gross carrying amount (exposures) with unknown use of proceeds of 
companies that fall under the NFRD in corporate financing and those exposures with known use of proceeds 
that are aligned with EU Taxonomy.

heading: Scope 1 -2 emissions
start_phrase: 50. a Emission of the Group preparing consolidated financial statements: emissions derived from the assets listed in the balance sheet of entities belonging to the consolidated accounting group according to IFRS, in a financial control approach, including emissions derived from assets under IFRS 16.
summary:
- Outlines OTP Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy compliance and references the bank’s key frameworks: OTP Group Green Loan Framework and Sustainable Finance Framework, which define green criteria for non-financial corporates alongside the Hungarian National Bank’s green capital requirement discount program.
- Notes the July 2023 update of the Green Loan Framework (with external SPO) approved by the Hungarian National Bank, enabling qualifying loans to count as “Category B” under the Hungarian green capital discount program.
- Defines the Green Loan Framework’s scope: nonresidential customers from large corporates to micro-enterprises, including municipalities and condominiums.
- Describes retail green lending foundations: the Hungarian National Bank’s Green housing capital requirement discount program and the NHP Green Home program, aligned with Hungarian and EU building-energy regulations (e.g., 9/2023 Decree and NZEB requirements).
- Explains differences between voluntary green portfolio metrics and mandatory EU Taxonomy GAR KPIs:
  - Voluntary GAR: centrally maintained, monthly monitored, includes EU- and non-EU clients and households beyond NFRD scope; expert-based eligibility assessment.
  - Mandatory GAR: semiannual, per EU 2021/2178; limited to NFRD corporates’ exposures with unknown use of proceeds and exposures with known EU Taxonomy-aligned use of proceeds.
- Details Scope 1 and 2 GHG accounting boundaries and methods:
  - Scope definitions for entities under financial control (50.a) and under operational control including investees/joint arrangements (50.b).
  - Not subject to emission trading schemes; minor data gaps estimated (e.g., invoices, refrigerants) with low uncertainty.
  - Scope 1 includes vehicle fuels, natural gas, air conditioners/server coolers; biogenic CH4 and N2O reported separately; IPCC AR6 factors used.
  - Scope 2 covers electricity and district heating; both location-based and market-based disclosed; renewable electricity via GoOs/RECs assigned zero market-based factor; share of contractual instruments reported.
  - Emission factor sources: national inventories/IPCC/EMEP-EEA/DEFRA; electricity residual mix via AIB or IFI grid factors; district heating via national sources or DEFRA; coverage of relevant GHGs clarified.
  - Agricultural non-mechanical GHGs disclosed using GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance and AKI calculator (IPCC 2006/2019 methods) for crop and livestock categories; biogenic emissions reported separately.
- Summarizes Scope 3 approach:
  - High-level estimation conducted for Categories 1–14 (PCAF Score 5/Option 3c); detailed calculation focuses on Category 15 (financed emissions).
- Describes financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15) methodology:
  - Uses PCAF Standard with attribution based on financing ratio (loan or exposure over financed asset/total assets).
  - Incorporates clients’ Scopes 1 and 2 (considered relatively more reliable) and acknowledges high uncertainty and speculative nature of clients’ Scope 3.
  - Highlights limited availability and assurance of client-reported emissions (data from 111 corporate clients, <4% of business loan portfolio) and intent to improve internal data management.
  - Uses external emission intensity datasets and proxies where needed:
    - PCAF/Exiobase for corporates (mostly excludes downstream Scope 3; 2019 data may cause overestimation due to price level changes).
    - PCAF/CRREM 2023 for commercial and residential real estate (combined Scopes 1+2; may differ from national data).
    - PCAF Motor Vehicle Loan Dataset for vehicle loans (by country and major vehicle classes).
    - Sovereign exposures per PCAF Standard sources.
  - Ensures consistency with Pillar 3 ESG risk disclosure methods and data.
text:
Scope 1 -2 emissions  
50. a Emission of the Group preparing consolidated financial statements: emissions derived from the assets 
listed in the balance sheet of entities belonging to the consolidated accounting group according to IFRS, in a 
financial control approach, including emissions derived from assets under IFRS 16.  
50. b Entities (except under 50. a) under operational control including investees (such as associates, joint 
ventures, or unconsolidated subsidiaries that are not fully consolidated in the financial statements of the 
consolidated accounting group), as well  as contractual arrangements that are joint arrangements not structured 
through an entity (i.e. jointly controlled operations and assets). Operational control:  Operational control (over 
an entity, site, operation or asset) is the situation where the undertaking has the ability to direct the operational 
activities and relationships of the entity, site, operation or asset.  
48. b The Group is not subject to emission trading schemes, therefore Scope 1 GHG emissions from regulated 
emission trading schemes are not relevant.  
The calculation methodology for Scope 1  and 2 emissions is the same for sections  50.a and 50.b.  
48. b In those instances when the invoice for the consumption is not available, estimates will be made for the 
missing items. Given the small amount of this emission item, this does not cause significant uncertainty in 
Scope 1 -2 emissions.  
48. a, AR 43. a The Scope 1 emission calculation includes emissions resulting from fuel/energy consumption 
of vehicles, natural gas, and the use of air conditioners and server coolers. CH4 and N2O content of biogenic 
emissions is calculated separately from  the Scope 1 emissions. Ratio of biofuel consumption is calculated by 
using default values; If the fuel consumed has a different biofuel -content, then individual ratios are used.   
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  258 48. b If the quantity of emissions from air conditioners and server coolers is not available, an estimate will be 
made. This does not cause a high degree of uncertainty in Scope 1 emissions, considering the small amount 
of this type of emission.  
For the calculation the latest IPCC report is used, which is currently the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6).  
The Group discloses non-mechanical GHG emissions related to agricultural production in accordance with the 
GHG Protocol Agricultural Guidance, the calculation calculation was carried out using a calculator developed 
by AKI Agrárközgazdasági Nonprofit Kft. The emission source categories considered in the calculator were 
determined in accordance with the GHG Protocol, and the methods were developed based on the methodology 
published in 2006 by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), taking into account the 2019 
amendments (IPCC 2006, IPCC 2019). The calculator quantifies CO2, CH4, and N2O emissions related to 
crop production and livestock farming. For crop production, the following were determined: N2O emissions 
from the use of synthetic and organic fertilizers; CO2  emissions from the use of urea and CAN -type fertilizers; 
CO2 emissions from soil liming; N2O emissions from crop residues; and indirect N2O emissions (from 
atmospheric deposition and nitrate leaching). For livestock farming, CH4 emissions from animal dige stion and 
CH4 and N2O emissions from manure management were determined.  
AR43. c Biogenic emissions are calculated separately from other Scope 1 emissions.  
Scope 2 emissions are related to electricity and district heating consumption. OTP Group discloses Scope 2 
emissions separately as location -based and market -based emissions.  
Sources of emission factors:  
Scope 1 : Emissions from mineral and biofuels, as well as natural gas: local NIR (National Inventory Report) 
or IPCC 2006 guidelines. Fuel calorific value: local NIRs or EMEP/EEA air pollutant emission inventory 
guidebook. In Slovenia, the Slovenian Environmental Agency. Non -biogenic emissions from biofuels: DEFRA. 
Other fuels: DEFRA or another credible source from the member company. The emission factors used 
comprehensively cover all greenhouse gases.  
Scope 2 : Electricity: market -based emission factors are provided by utility providers, in the absence of which 
the Group uses the residual mix factors of the AIB (Association of Issuing Body) where available. In countries 
where residual mix is not available, the local and market factors are the same, with the source of emission 
factors being the IFI harmonized grid factors. The emission factor for electricity includes only CO2.  
For district heating, the Group uses the emission factor provided by MATÁSZSZ in Hungary, the Energy 
Institute Hrvoje Požar in Croatia, and Bureau Veritas in Slovenia. For other countries, the DEFRA factor is 
used. The local -based and market factors are th e same. The emission factors include all relevant greenhouse 
gases.  
For renewable electricity purchased through contractual instruments (Guarantees of Origins or Renewable 
Energy Certificates) the market -based emission factor applied is 0.  
AR 45. D. The share of contractual instruments is calculated as the total amount of electricity purchased from 
renewable contractual agreements, divided by the total amount of electricity purchased. Information about the 
types of contractual instruments is  determined in the Guarantees of Origins or Renewable Energy Certificates.  
AR 43. Biogenic emissions related to Scope 2 are not relevant for the Group.  
AR 46. Scope 3 emissions :  
AR 46 c, d., i. OTP Group  has conducted a high -level estimation of Scope 3 GHG emissions for Categories 1 -
14 using the PCAF Score 5 / Option 3c methodology. Therefore, the calculation exclusively focuses on 
Category 15. MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  259

title: Category 15 emissions – emissions financed through investments
heading: Category 15 emissions – emissions financed through investments
start_phrase: AR 46. A., b. Scope 3 / Category 15 GHG emissions of OTP Group are those that are related to emissions of clients to which OTP Group provides funds in the form of loans or equity, or through investing into their securities.
summary:
- Financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15): OTP Group attributes a share of clients’ GHG emissions to the bank proportional to the financing ratio (attribution factor). It includes clients’ Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions, but OTP considers Scope 1–2 estimates relatively reliable and Scope 3 highly uncertain/speculative.

- Methodology and data: Financed emissions quantified per PCAF Standard, as required by ESRS/CSRD, and aligned with the Group’s Pillar 3 ESG risk disclosures. Due to scarce client-reported data (emissions reported by only 111 corporate clients, <4% of portfolio, mostly unaudited), OTP estimates borrower emissions using financial data and external emission intensity factors:
  - Corporates: PCAF/Exiobase 2019 intensity data; may omit most downstream Scope 3 and can bias results (possible Scope 3 underestimation; potential overestimation from using 2019 intensities with higher 2023/24 price levels while national emissions largely stagnated).
  - Real estate: PCAF/CRREM 2023 building intensities (combined Scope 1+2), which can differ from national data.
  - Vehicle loans: PCAF Motor Vehicle Loan dataset by country and main vehicle types.
  - Sovereign exposures: per PCAF sovereign guidance.
  - Proxies used where country/asset data are missing. OTP plans to analyze internal data management gaps as CSRD expands data availability.

- GHG intensity ratio: Calculated as Total GHG emissions (tCO2e) / Net revenue (million HUF), reported on both location-based and market-based bases. Net revenue follows the 2024 consolidated IFRS (interest income and similar + fee and commission income + other operating income).

- ESG risk management: The Group integrates ESG/climate risks across risk types (credit, market, liquidity, operational) and aligns with the Hungarian National Bank’s Green Recommendation 10/2022. Compliance is reported to the Board, Management Committee, ESG Committee, and Risk Management Committee. The Group monitors EBA/ECB expectations; ECB has direct supervision over DSK Bank (Bulgaria) and OTP Bank Slovenia. DSK, OTP Slovenia, and OTP Croatia have integrated ESG risk factors per local supervisory expectations.

- Governance and internal frameworks: Sustainability-related risk management is guided by a suite of internal, non-public policies, including governance and organizational regulations, risk strategy and appetite, credit and market risk policies, collateral and operational risk policies, lending guidelines, remuneration and performance rules, and a CEO directive on greenwashing risk.
text:
Category 15 emissions – emissions financed through investments   
AR 46. A., b.  Scope 3 / Category 15 GHG emissions of OTP Group are those that are related to emissions of 
clients to which OTP Group provides funds in the form of loans or equity, or through investing into their 
securities. The general logic of allocating such emissions  to the bank is the following: we take the clients’ 
(borrowers’) total GHG emissions, then we allocate them to the Group in proportion to the financing ratio of 
the client / borrower (e.g. the client’s loan outstanding / the client’s total assets or the cl ient’s loan outstanding 
/ financed asset of the client.  
When covering clients’ (borrowers’) GHG emissions, all emission types have to be included as requested by 
the relevant EU -regulation: Scope 1 emissions (resulting from fossil fuels that the client burns directly), Scope 
2 emissions (resulting from the prod uction of electricity and heating that the client uses) and Scope 3 emissions 
(all emission that arise in the client’s supply chain). The reliability by which these estimations can be measured 
or at least estimated is very different: Scope 1 emissions coul d ideally be even measured or at least estimated 
with a relatively low level of uncertainty, if client would measure and report them (which is not the case for 
most OTP Group clients). Scope 2 emissions cannot be measured, only estimated with some uncertai nty: 
while the volume of electricity or heat used by the client could be ideally measured and reported by the client 
(though it is not the case for the bulk of OTP Group’s portfolio), the underlying GHG emissions of such energy 
used can only be estimated, but not measured (as those depend on the actual fuel mix of the grid from which 
the client bought such energy). Scope 3 emissions of clients can only be estimated with a very large level of 
uncertainty, as even the clients do not fully control, and thus ha ve not enough information of the emission 
profile of their supply chain (except for a few exceptions). Therefore, OTP Group considers only estimations 
on clients’ Scope 1 and 2 emission indicators as relatively reliable ones, whereas we deem estimations on  
Scope 3 emissions of clients (borrowers) to be completely speculative.   
OTP Group quantifies its financed emissions based on the methodology described by the PCAF Standard86 
as requested by relevant EU regulation (ESRS/CSRD).  The essence of the approach is that a bank providing 
funds to a client has to use the client’s GHG emission as a basis and then allocate part of it to the bank’s 
financed GHG emissions based on the clie nt’s financing ratio (called also the “attribution factor”, equal to the 
loan provided to the client / value of the financed asset or the total assets of the client). This financing ratio 
defines the share of GHG emission of the borrower which the financin g bank can be made responsible for 
(according to the underlying regulation). GHG emission of the clients should be quantified on emission values 
measured and reported by the client. However, by end of 2024, most borrowers of OTP Group have not 
reported (an d many of them not even measured) their own GHG emissions. In fact, OTP Group has reported 
emission data only from 111 of its corporate clients (accounting for less than 4% of the total business loan 
portfolio) and even most of these are not audited by an independent third party. The availability of reported 
corporate emission data might improve somewhat as CSRD will apply to more and more companies. As the 
first step to enhance the accessibility and quality of data, OTP Bank plans to analyze the gap regard ing internal 
data management processes.  
Therefore, OTP Group had to prepare its own estimations for its borrowers’ GHG emissions. These estimations 
were based on the financial figures (such as revenues and total assets) of clients (borrowers) and GHG 
emission intensity factors (e.g. on emissions  / revenue by activity types) from external data providers. OTP 
Bank – as a PCAF signatory – has access to emission intensity factors that were made available by PCAF.87 
However, the PCAF -databases do not provide emission intensity factors for all countries and/or asset types 
which are relevant for OTP Group: in such cases, proxies of similar (in economic and environmental terms) 
countries or asset types were used.  
OTP Group prepares the estimate of financed GHG emissions disclosed in this document based on the same 
methods and data as in its Pillar 3 disclosures on ESG risks.
 
86 PCAF (2022). The Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard Part A: Financed Emissions. Second Edition.  
87 In case of corporate loans and bonds and equity exposures, OTP Group relied on the emission intensity factors of the PCAF/Exi obase dataset. 
Emission intensity data in this dataset relies on environmentally extended IO tables, and thus does not cover (most ly) downstream Scope 3 emissions. 
Therefore, our estimations on clients’ Scope 3 emissions might be underestimated – however, there are no reliable estimations on downstream emission 
intensity factors for a wide spectrum of industries and countries accordi ng to our knowledge. Intensity data in the PCAF/Exiobase dataset is from the 
year 2019 as it was made available by PCAF in 2024 – relying on data from 2019 to estimate borrowers’ emissions in 2023/2024 might lead to some 
overestimation as national emission s (in countries where OTP Group is present) mostly stagnated between 2019 -2024, whereas price levels – and thus 
average sizes of loans or average levels of revenues – have gone up.  
For commercial and residential real estate loans, OTP Group relied on emission intensity factors of residential and commercia l buildings (either per 
building or per m2) the PCAF/CRREM (Carbon Risk Real Estate Monitor) dataset. Data in this dataset is from the year 2023. It has to be noted th at 
emission intensity factors from this dataset sometimes differs from that published by national authorities. Also, PCAF/CRREM does not provide data 
separately for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions of buildings, only for the combination of them.  
For vehicle loans, OTP Group relied on emission intensity factors from the PCAF Motor Vehicle Loan Dataset. Although this dat aset provides intensity 
factors for a wide range of different vehicles and car types, OTP Group relied only on the emission intensi ty by country and main vehicle types (passenger 
car, van, heavy vehicle).  
For the sovereign exposures, OTP Group relied on the exact same data sources as they were provided in the chapter on “Soverei gn debt” of the PCAF 
Standard.   
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  260

title: ESG risk management - Introduction
heading: 2.4. ESG risk management
start_phrase: The Group pays particular attention to managing ESG risks and implementing climate protection aspects into business practices.
summary: Introduction to OTP Banking Group’s ESG risk management framework, detailing integration of climate and environmental risks—particularly those related to green loans—across credit, market, liquidity, and operational risk in line with prudent banking laws. Adequacy is benchmarked against the Hungarian National Bank’s Green Recommendation 10/2022 (VIII.2.), with regular compliance reporting to the Board of Directors, Management Committee, ESG Committee, and Risk Management Committee. The Group aligns with EBA and ECB expectations; the ECB (JST) directly supervises DSK Bank (Bulgaria) and OTP Bank Slovenia, and DSK, OTP Slovenia, and OTP Croatia have embedded ESG risk factors per local supervisors. Practices also draw on NGFS, GHG Protocol, and PCAF voluntary standards.
text:
ESG risk management  
The Group pays particular attention to managing ESG risks and implementing climate protection aspects into 
business practices. The Banking Group's risk management and business area pay special attention to 
integrating various risks related to green loans.  
OTP Bank has detailed risk management policies covering all types of risks (credit, market, liquidity, 
operational), which are in line with the laws regulating prudent banking operations:  
The assessment of the adequacy of ESG risk management is primarily based on the recommendation 10/2022 
(VIII.2.) issued by the Hungarian National Bank (Green Recommendation), which describes the expectations 
for credit institutions regarding climate change  and environmental risks, as well as the enforcement of 
sustainability aspects. The recommendation sets specific expectations for managing environmental risks. 
Compliance with the Green Recommendation is regularly reported to the Board of Directors, the Ma nagement 
Committee, the ESG Committee, and the Risk Management Committee.  
The Bank also monitors the supervisory and regulatory expectations of the European Banking Authority (EBA) 
and the European Central Bank (ECB). The ECB has direct supervisory authority (JST) over DSK Bank in 
Bulgaria and OTP Bank Slovenia, so compliance wi th these institutions' expectations receives special attention 
in examining and managing environmental and climate risks. DSK Bank, OTP Bank Slovenia and OTP Bank 
Croatia have integrated ESG Risk factors into their risk management system with local supervi sory 
expectations.  
The Bank manages its sustainability -related risk management guidelines based on the following non -public 
documents:  
• Organizational and Operational Regulations  
• OTP Banking Group Governance Regulations  
• The internal defense lines system at OTP Bank  
• The Rules of the Remuneration Policy of OTP Bank and the Banking Group  
• The Rules of the Performance Measurement and Evaluation System of OTP Bank and the Banking 
Group subsidiaries  
• The Guidelines for the Leading Bodies and Standing Committees of the Banking Group Credit 
Institutions  
• Group Credit Risk Policy  
• Group -Level Trading Market Risk Management  
• Market Risk and Foreign Exchange Risk Management for the Trading Book  
• OTP Group Risk Strategy  
• OTP Group Risk Appetite Statement  
• Corporate Lending Policy / Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP)  
• The CEO's directive on managing the greenwashing risk of OTP Bank  
• Corporate Client Risk Management Manual (OTP Bank)  
• OTP Banking Group Risk Appetite Framework  
• Collateral Valuation Policy  
• Operational Risk Management Policy  
 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  261 The Bank develops its ESG risk management practices based on the following voluntary standard 
expectations:  
• NGFS, The Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System  
• GHG, Greenhouse Gas Protocol  
• PCAF, Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials

title: ESG Risk Management Function and Integration of ESG Risks into Risk Management Procedure
heading: 2.4.1. ESG Risk Management Function and Integration of ESG Risks into Risk Management Procedure
start_phrase: OTP Bank has incorporated ESG risks into its group -level risk management guidelines and procedures, enabling the identification and management of these risks to minimize emerging credit, reputational, regulatory, and legal risks.
summary:
- Establishes OTP Bank’s ESG risk management approach, aligned with voluntary standards: NGFS, GHG Protocol, and PCAF.
- Describes integration of ESG risks across OTP Group’s risk ecosystem: Group Risk Strategy, Risk Appetite Statement (RAS), risk-type frameworks, and Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines (OLLP), with a gradual approach to ESG-related risk limits.
- Introduces a 2023–2025 group-level ESG risk strategy to deepen implementation and awareness, including:
  - Climate and Environmental Materiality Assessment of physical and transition risks over short (<1 year), medium (1–5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons.
  - Enhancements to ESG elements of risk appetite, setting limits to support a sustainable portfolio.
  - Development of a Group-level Climate and Environmental Risk Heatmap and implementation of relevant environmental factors.
- Details corporate credit risk management for ESG:
  - Since 2021, application of an ESG framework in corporate lending built on an exclusion list, a sectoral ESG risk heatmap (by NACE), and client/transaction-level ESG risk assessments.
  - Special methodology for motorized leasing based on vehicle emission standards.
  - Ongoing method refinement as data and methodologies improve.
- Notes regulatory alignment in Hungary: compliance preparation for MNB’s phased 2025 requirements for an ESG examination framework and minimum ESG due diligence questionnaire.
- Outlines OLLP corporate lending guidelines (excluding Uzbek and Russian subsidiaries) that embed environmental/climate risk criteria and financial risk assessment rules; includes guidance for financing renewable energy projects.
- Mentions an internal, non-public coal mining and coal-based energy financing guideline under review, with intent to publish after completion.
- Emphasizes the aim to mitigate credit, reputational, regulatory, and legal risks through comprehensive ESG risk integration.
text:
4.1.  ESG Risk Management Function and Integration of ESG Risks into Risk Management 
Procedure  
OTP Bank has incorporated ESG risks into its group -level risk management guidelines and procedures, 
enabling the identification and management of these risks to minimize emerging credit, reputational, regulatory, 
and legal risks. ESG risk management within  OTP Group is integrated into various levels of the risk ecosystem: 
OTP Group Risk Strategy, OTP Group Risk Appetite Statement, the risk management frameworks for different 
risk types, and the Operational Lending Limits and Guidelines. OTP Group applies a gradual approach to ESG -
related risk limits, and the Risk Appetite Statement and Group -Level Operational Lending Limits and 
Guidelines (OLLP) already include such restrictions.  
In connection with the group -level risk strategy  for 2023 -2025, a group -level risk strategy with ESG relevance 
will be defined, aiming for a higher level of implementation of ESG risk factors. The ESG risk strategy will 
define additional ESG -level focus programs to strengthen ESG risk awareness. The ESG  risk strategy includes 
assessing the short (<1 year), medium (1 -5 years), and long -term (>5 years)88 physical and transitional risk 
factors resulting from climate change in the portfolio (Climate and Environmental Materiality Assessment) for 
significant sectors. As a result, it will further develop the ESG -relevant parts of the risk appetite and set limi ts 
to serve the Bank's long -term sustainable portfolio more effectively. The assessment also supports the 
preparation of the Group -Level Climate and Environmental Risk Heatmap and the implementation of all 
identified relevant "E" (environmental) factors.

title: Credit Risk - Introduction
heading: 2.4.2. Credit Risk
start_phrase: To manage the credit risk aspect of ESG risks, OTP Group has been applying its ESG risk management framework in corporate lending since 2021.
summary: OTP Group’s corporate lending credit risk ESG framework (in place since 2021) comprises an ESG exclusion list, a sectoral ESG risk heatmap aligned to NACE activities, and client- and transaction-level ESG risk assessment with due diligence triggers; motorized leasing exposures are categorized by engine environmental impact using European vehicle emission standards. ESG considerations are embedded in lending decisions and methods are evolving with data. The Corporate Lending Policy/Operational Lending Limits and Policies (excluding Uzbek and Russian subsidiaries) include environmental and climate risk guidelines, financial risk assessment rules based on environmental risks, and renewable energy financing and examination frameworks; an internal, non-public coal mining and coal-based energy financing guideline is under review and intended to be published. Consistent with EBA expectations on time horizons, the Group applies limits within the ESG credit process, including a group-level limit tied to the exclusion list and, since 2023 in Hungary and certain subsidiaries, a numerical cap on the share of new high-ESG-risk transactions; these non-public limits are recorded in the Risk Appetite Statement or Corporate Lending Policy, monitored monthly and quarterly, and are being expanded. From 2023, monthly group-level ESG credit risk exposure reports for the corporate loan portfolio are provided to the Credit and Limit Committee and quarterly to the Board of Directors. OTP is preparing to meet the Hungarian National Bank’s phased 2025 requirements for a special examination framework and a minimum ESG due-diligence questionnaire for environmental and climate risk assessment.
text:
Credit Risk Management  
To manage the credit risk aspect of ESG risks, OTP Group has been applying its ESG risk management 
framework in corporate lending since 2021. The main elements of the framework are the ESG exclusion list, 
the sectoral ESG risk heatmap, and the ESG risk ass essment.  
The ESG exclusion list defines activities in which OTP Group does not participate directly due to their 
controversial nature and impact. The sectoral ESG risk heatmap includes the ESG risk categorization of each 
economic activity in the NACE classification, considering the environmental and social impact of the respective 
industry.  
The ESG risk assessment includes determining ESG risk categories at client and transaction levels, including 
client due diligence in predefined cases. The Group applies a different method for leasing transactions where 
the financed asset is motorized; in t hese cases, the ESG risk category is determined based on the estimated 
environmental impact of the asset's engine (considering European vehicle emission standards). ESG aspects 
are considered in individual corporate lending decisions. The methods are conti nuously developed in line with 
the expansion of available data and methodologies.  
In corporate lending – as for the Hungarian operations – the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) prescribes the 
application of a special examination framework and a minimum ESG questionnaire for client due diligence 
related to environmental and climate risk asse ssment, starting from 2025 with a phased implementation. The 
Bank is working to ensure compliance with the recommendation according to the schedule outlined in the 
recommendation .  
In the Corporate Lending Policy / Operational Lending Limits and Policies (OLLP) – with the exception of the 
Uzbek and Russian subsidiary banks – lending guidelines from an environmental and climate risk perspective, 
as well as financial risk assessment gu idelines based on environmental risks, have been formulated. As part 
of the policy, financing guidelines and examination frameworks related to renewable energy production, a key 
element of green lending, are also included. OTP Group currently has an intern al, non -public guideline related 
to financing coal mining and coal -based energy production activities. The review is currently in progress, and 
upon its completion, the Group intends to make this policy public.  
 
88 These time horizons are different from the time horizons used in OTP Group, in line with the EBA's expectations.  

 MANAGEMENT REPORT (CONSOLIDATED ) 
INTEGRATED ANNUAL REPORT 2024  262 Regarding credit risk, the group also applies limits related to the corporate ESG risk management process. A 
group -level limit is applied to the ESG exclusion list, and in 2023 a new numerical limit was introduced in the 
Hungarian operations and certain su bsidiaries to limit the proportion of new transactions with high ESG risk 
ratings within new risk -taking. The range of applied limits is gradually expanding, and the limits are recorded 
in the Risk Appetite Statement or the Corporate Lending Policy, curren tly not public. Compliance with the limits 
is regularly monitored on a quarterly and monthly basis. The methodology is continuously developed, with 
plans to introduce additional risk limits and apply ESG -specific lending guidelines.  
From 2023, monthly internal reports on group -level ESG credit risk exposure are prepared for the corporate 
loan portfolio for the Credit and Limit Committee, and quarterly for the Board of Directors.

title: Collateral management - Introduction
heading: Collateral management
start_phrase: In the case of collateralized commercial real estate, the ESG assessment methodology developed by OTP Mortgage Bank has been applied in the Hungarian operations since February 2023.
summary: Overview of OTP Group’s ESG-based collateral management: Since February 2023, OTP Mortgage Bank applies an ESG assessment to collateralized commercial real estate in Hungarian operations, reflecting significant CRE exposure and prioritizing ESG evaluation. The current rating uses simplified E, S, G factors, with planned expansion aligned to the C&E Materiality Assessment. ESG data fields were added to the corporate loan registry and are partially auto-populated from the state Lechner Knowledge Center, with energy efficiency of collateral as a key indicator. Methodology sharing with subsidiaries is underway; ESG frameworks for vehicle-related collateral are being implemented per agreed timelines. text:
Collateral management  
In the case of collateralized commercial real estate, the ESG assessment methodology developed by OTP 
Mortgage Bank has been applied in the Hungarian operations since February 2023. This is due to the bank’s 
significant exposure to commercial real estate, where the proper ESG -relevant evaluation is a primary 
consideration.  
The current rating is based on simplified ESG factors (E, S, G), and the general factors will be expanded based 
on the relevant factors detailed in the C&E Materiality Assessment. ESG data fields have been created in the 
bank's corporate loan registry syst em, and the process of populating these with actual content is partially 
automated from the information available in the state Lechner Knowledge Center database, with the most 
important data being the indicator of the energy efficiency of the collateral. T he sharing of the collateral ESG 
methodology with subsidiaries is currently ongoing.  
For subsidiaries, the implementation of ESG methodologies for collateral related to vehicles is in progress 
according to pre -agreed deadlines. Merkantil Bank has its own ESG methodology for leasing assets according 
to the appendix of the current Group Cred it Risk Policy. In this regard, the methodologies presented below 
show the practice of OTP Bank, and the implementation in subsidiaries is currently ongoing.

Immovable property

Movable Property  
For movable collateral relating to vehicles, OTP Bank has also developed an IT -supported framework for
